Paanch points, do features; doosra feature decoy (bekaar). XᵀX = [[15, 1], [1, 2]], Xᵀy = [29.4, 2.3].

  1. OLS (no penalty): w = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy = (1.9483, 0.1759)
  2. Ridge, λ = 2: w = (XᵀX + 2I)⁻¹Xᵀy; [[17, 1], [1, 4]] ka det = 68 − 1 = 67 → w₁ = (4 × 29.4 − 2.3)/67 = 115.3/67 = 1.7209, w₂ = (−29.4 + 17 × 2.3)/67 = 9.7/67 = 0.1448
  3. Lasso, λ = 2: w = (1.8933, 0.0000) (w₂ = 0 rakh ke: w₁ = (29.4 − λ/2)/15 = 28.4/15 = 1.8933)

Ridge ne dono chhote kiye, koi zero nahi. Lasso ne decoy ko exactly 0 kar diya aur asli feature ko kam chheda (1.8933 vs ridge ka 1.7209). "Weak weights become exactly zero. Strong weights lose less than under L2."

PyTorch me L1 (aur manual L2) — loss me khud jodo

PyTorch optimizers me L1 ka koi argument nahi hai, isliye L1 hamesha loss me manually jodte hain. Same tareeke se manual L2 bhi:

PyTorch · manual L1 / L2 penalty in the training loop

# model, criterion, optimizer pehle se bane hain
l1_lambda = 1e-4
l2_lambda = 1e-4

for xb, yb in train_loader:
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    outputs = model(xb)
    loss = criterion(outputs, yb)

    # L1: saare parameters ke |w| ka sum
    l1_penalty = sum(p.abs().sum() for p in model.parameters())
    # L2: saare parameters ke w^2 ka sum
    l2_penalty = sum(p.pow(2).sum() for p in model.parameters())

    loss = loss + l1_lambda * l1_penalty          # L1 chahiye to ye
    # loss = loss + l2_lambda * l2_penalty        # L2 chahiye to ye

    loss.backward()        # autograd khud sign(w) aur 2w wale gradients nikaal lega
    optimizer.step()

# Sirf weights (biases nahi) penalize karne ho to:
l1_weights_only = sum(p.abs().sum() for name, p in model.named_parameters()
                      if 'weight' in name)
  • p.abs() = elementwise |w|; .sum() = tensor ka total. Bahar wala sum(... for p in model.parameters()) saari layers jodta hai → ek scalar tensor.
  • Penalty tensor graph ka hissa hai, isliye loss.backward() uska gradient (L1: λ·sign(w), L2: 2λw) apne aap jod deta hai.
  • model.named_parameters() → (naam, tensor) pairs, jaise '0.weight', '0.bias'; isse biases chhod sakte ho.

Ab dekho L1 aur L2 asal me weights ke saath kya karte hain. 8 input features, lekin sirf pehle 3 kaam ke (true weights 3, −2, 1.5, baaki 0):

PyTorch · L1 vs L2 on a model with 5 useless features

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.optim as optim

torch.manual_seed(0)
X = torch.randn(200, 8)                                   # 8 input features
true_w = torch.tensor([3.0, -2.0, 1.5, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0])    # sirf pehle 3 kaam ke
y = (X @ true_w + 0.5 * torch.randn(200)).unsqueeze(1)    # (200,) -> (200, 1)

def fit(penalty, lam):
    torch.manual_seed(1)
    model = nn.Linear(8, 1)
    optimizer = optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.05)
    criterion = nn.MSELoss()
    for epoch in range(500):
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss = criterion(model(X), y)
        if penalty == "L1":
            loss = loss + lam * model.weight.abs().sum()       # lam * sum|w|
        elif penalty == "L2":
            loss = loss + lam * model.weight.pow(2).sum()      # lam * sum w^2
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
    return model.weight.data.squeeze()

for penalty in ["none", "L1", "L2"]:
    w = fit(penalty, lam=0.1)
    print(f"{penalty:4s}:", [round(v, 3) for v in w.tolist()])

Output

none: [3.044, -1.952, 1.472, -0.053, -0.02, 0.007, -0.005, 0.001]
L1  : [2.982, -1.899, 1.42, -0.002, 0.003, -0.002, 0.001, 0.001]
L2  : [2.709, -1.746, 1.34, -0.053, -0.024, 0.029, 0.0, 0.012]
  • L1: 5 bekaar weights ±0.003 ke andar (zero pe "chipak" gaye), aur kaam ke weights lagbhag poore bache (2.982, −1.899, 1.42).
  • L2: kaam ke weights zyada shrink hue (2.709, −1.746, 1.34) aur bekaar weights chhote lekin zinda (−0.053, 0.029, 0.012...).
  • L1 ke "zero" exactly 0.000 kyun nahi? Plain SGD me har step ±ηλ = ±0.005 ka fixed kadam lagta hai, to weight zero ke aas-paas aage-peeche jhoolta rehta hai. Exact zero ke liye clipping / soft-thresholding (proximal) step chahiye — worksheet: "With plain gradient steps a weight can jump back and forth across zero. Libraries handle this; the lab clips at zero."

Ek aur slide point — robustness: L1 > L2. Squared cheez me bade outlier ka cost bahut tezi se (slide ne "exponentially" likha; asal me quadratically) badhta hai, absolute me linearly. Isliye squared form outliers pe zyada mehnat (zyada react) karta hai → kam robust. (Ye baat loss functions MSE vs MAE pe bhi same lagti hai — Chapter 11.)

Exam Radar

  • L1 = Lasso: penalty λΣ|w|; gradient λ·sign(w) (constant size); update w − ηg − ηλ·sign(w).
  • L1 → sparsity: exact zeros → feature selection, compression. L2 → small but non-zero.
  • |w| non-differentiable at 0; subgradient ∈ [−1, 1].
  • Soft-thresholding: Sλ(z) = sign(z)·max(|z| − λ, 0).
  • PyTorch me L1 ke liye optimizer argument nahi; loss me sum(p.abs().sum() for p in model.parameters()).
  • Robustness to outliers: L1 > L2. Sparsity: L1 > L2.

Galti mat karna

  • L1 ka gradient λw nahi, λ·sign(w) hai — weight ke size pe depend nahi karta.
  • Correlated features me Lasso aksar ek ko chunta hai aur doosre ko zero karta hai (dono ko barabar nahi rakhta).

Dimaag me aise baitha lo

L2 divide karta hai (sab chhote, koi zero nahi). L1 subtract karta hai (kamzor seedha zero).

19.4 Geometry — L2 ka circle, L1 ka diamond

Regularization ko ek budget ki tarah bhi soch sakte ho: "data loss minimize karo, lekin weights ek budget ke andar rahein". L2 me budget w₁² + w₂² ≤ t² — ek circle (disk). L1 me |w₁| + |w₂| ≤ t — ek diamond jiske kone (corners) axes pe hain.

Data loss ke contours (barabar loss wali lines) unregularized best point ŵ ke around ellipses hain. Ellipse ko dheere-dheere bada karte jao; jahan wo pehli baar budget region ko chhooti hai, wahi regularized solution hai.

  • Circle gol hai, koi kona nahi. Ellipse usse kisi bhi direction se chhoo sakti hai, aur exactly axis pe chhoona ek khaas sanyog hai → dono weights non-zero.
  • Diamond ke nukeele kone axes pe hain aur bahar ki taraf nikle hue hain. Badhti ellipse sabse pehle aksar kone se takraati hai → wahan ek coordinate exactly 0. Zyada dimensions me diamond ke aur bhi zyada kone/edges axes pe hote hain → aur zyada zeros. Yahi sparsity ka geometric reason hai.
  • Budget tight (λ bada) → circle/diamond chhota → weights zyada shrink.

Dimaag me aise baitha lo

Gol roti ko ellipse kahin bhi chhoo le; samosa (diamond) ko pehle uska kona hi chubhta hai — aur kona axis pe hai, matlab ek weight zero.

19.5 L1 vs L2 — poori comparison, Elastic Net, kab kya

FeatureL1 (Lasso)L2 (Ridge / weight decay)
PenaltyλΣ|w|λΣw² (ya (λ/2)Σw²)
UsesAbsolute weightSquared weight
Gradient of penaltyλ·sign(w) — constant size2λw (ya λw) — proportional to w
Update ka asarFixed amount subtractFixed fraction multiply (decay)
Exact zerosHaan, common (sparse)Lagbhag kabhi nahi
Feature selectionHaan (automatic)Nahi
Weights ka patternKuch bade, baaki 0 (0.8, 0, 1, 0)Sab chhote, spread (0.3, 0.1, 0.3, 0.2)
Constraint shapeDiamondCircle / sphere
Differentiable at 0?Nahi (kona)Haan (smooth)
Closed formNahi (soft-thresholding / iterative)Haan: (XᵀX + λI)⁻¹Xᵀy
Outlier robustness (slide)Zyada robustKam robust
Correlated featuresEk ko chunta, baaki zeroCredit baant deta hai
Tuning"Cliff" — thoda λ badla, bahut weights achanak zeroGradual, aasaan
PyTorchLoss me manual: p.abs().sum()weight_decay= (ya manual p.pow(2).sum())
Deep learning meSpecific jobs: first-layer feature selection, compressionDefault

Elastic Net = L1 + L2 dono ek saath: L + λ₁Σ|w| + λ₂Σw². Jab thoda sparsity bhi chahiye aur correlated features me credit bhi baantna hai (Lasso akela ek ko chunta hai; elastic net group ko saath rakhta hai).

Kab kya use karein? (worksheet 09, 3.6)

  • L2 is the default in deep learning. Hidden neurons meaningful "features" nahi hote; deep nets pattern ko kai weights me thoda-thoda baant ke rakhte hain — L2 sabko zinda aur chhota rakhta hai, bilkul wahi regime. λ ke saath gradual change, tune karna aasaan. Aur har framework me "weight decay" yahi hai.
  • L1 is a tool for specific jobs: first layer pe feature selection (jab lagta hai bahut inputs bekaar hain), compression (sparse model chhota aur fast).
  • L1 ki "cliff": worksheet lab me λ = 0.003 ne 90% weights zero kar diye phir bhi model overfit karta raha (bache hue thode weights islands bana lete hain); λ = 0.01 ne 99% zero kiye, still overfit; λ = 0.03 pe jaake regularize hua (sirf 10 weights bache). Lekin L2 0.03 ne saare 2751 weights chhote rakhe — validation loss ~0.64 vs L1 ka ~0.54 us problem pe (jise sirf kuch weights chahiye the). Zyada real problems me, jahan bahut weights thoda-thoda signal rakhte hain, L2 jeetta hai.
  • Linear model, bahut correlated features: lasso ya elastic net, dropout nahi (worksheet "which knob").

Dimaag me aise baitha lo

L1 = "kaun zaroori hai?" chunta hai. L2 = "sab thoda-thoda" rakhta hai. Elastic Net = dono ka mix.

19.6 λ ka asar — kitna regularization?

λ ek dial hai. λ = 0 → koi regularization nahi (overfit ka khatra). λ bahut bada → model sirf weights chhote karne me laga, data ignore → underfit. Beech me kahin sweet spot. Bishop PRML fig. 1.7 bhi yahi dikhata hai: "Large λ underfits; small λ overfits."

Chalo numbers se samjhein — degree-9 polynomial + ridge, λ sweep (numpy se compute kiya)

12 noisy points (sin(2πx) + noise σ = 0.25), degree-9 polynomial (10 coefficients), ridge penalty λΣw², 300 validation points:

λTrain MSEVal MSELargest |w|Diagnosis
00.02200.215728171.95Overfit (bade weights!)
1e-60.05610.1353247.31Kam overfit
1e-40.10990.114415.39Achha
1e-30.12290.11369.57Best (sweet spot)
1e-20.18020.15213.44Thoda underfit
1e-10.21440.20121.10Underfit
10.29290.33230.45Underfit
100.40020.48780.09Bahut underfit (curve lagbhag flat)

Training MSE λ ke saath hamesha badhta hai; validation MSE pehle girta (0.2157 → 0.1136) phir badhta (→ 0.4878). Largest weight 28172 se 0.09 tak — λ jitna bada, weights utne chhote. Wahi U-curve, bas x-axis pe ab capacity ki jagah λ (ulta direction).

  • λ ko log scale pe try karo: 0.003, 0.01, 0.03, 0.1 (worksheet) ya 1e-5 … 1e-3 (labs). Coarse pehle, phir fine.
  • Hamesha validation readout se chuno, test se kabhi nahi.
  • Worksheet lab: L2 λ = 0.03 → arcs bache, islands gayab; λ = 0.3 → boundary lagbhag seedhi line, training curve high: underfitting. Regularisation worksheet: λ = 10 pe dono errors high → underfitting.
  • Stacking has diminishing returns: har method usi gap pe hamla karta hai. Gap band ho gaya to aur method jodne se model underfit me chala jaata hai. Worksheet Lab 6: L2 0.03 + dropout 0.5 ek saath → train acc 80, val acc 77 = underfitting; "One well-chosen method beats two."

Galti mat karna

  • "Zyada regularization = hamesha behtar" — nahi. Underfit model me regularization kam karna hai (18.2).

Dimaag me aise baitha lo

λ = namak. Zero: pheeka overfit. Mutthi bhar: kadwa underfit. Chutki bhar: perfect.

19.7 Early Stopping — ratta shuru hone se pehle ruk jao

Kahani

Maa chai bana rahi hai. Har minute ek chammach se chakh ke dekhti hai. Pehle 4 minute chai har baar behtar hoti gayi. 5th minute pe ekdum perfect. 6th minute pe thodi kadwi, 7th pe aur kadwi. Maa samajhdaar hai: "Ek minute ki kadwahat se ghabraana nahi, kabhi-kabhi chakhne me galti ho jaati hai. 3 minute tak sudhaar nahi hua to gas band." Aur agar unke paas magic hota, to wo 5th minute wali chai ka "photo" save karke wahi wapas parosti!

Yahi early stopping hai: validation loss = chai ka swaad, patience = 3 minute ka intezaar, best weights save + restore = perfect chai ki photocopy.

Course slide: "There is a point during training a large neural net when the model will stop generalizing (performing well on test/validation sets) and only focus on learning the statistical noise in the training dataset. Solution: stop whenever generalization error increases."

Definition

Early stopping: har epoch ke baad validation loss naapo. Jab tak gir raha hai, training chalu rakho. Jab wo sudharna band kar de (lagatar patience epochs tak koi naya best nahi), training rok do aur sabse kam validation loss wale epoch ke weights wapas load karo.

Formally: θ̂ = θt*, jahan t* = arg mint Lval(θt).

Training ke do phase hote hain (worksheet 09): pehle model pattern seekhta hai — dono losses girte hain. Phir noise yaad karne lagta hai — training loss girta rehta hai, validation loss rukta aur badhne lagta hai. Early stopping in dono phases ki seema (border) pe rukta hai. Worksheet lab me ye border epoch 73 pe tha (unregularised run, lowest validation loss).

Pehle hi bure epoch pe kyun nahi rukte? Patience

Validation loss noisy hota hai — ek epoch thoda kharab aane ka matlab ye nahi ki memorization shuru ho gaya. Pehle hi rise pe ruke to aksar bahut jaldi ruk jaoge. Isliye intezaar karte hain. Patience = lagatar kitne epochs bina naye best ke bardaasht karenge. Jab bhi naya best aaye, weights save karo aur counter 0 kar do.

Chalo numbers se samjhein — poora epoch table (worksheet 09, figure 4.2, patience = 3)

12 epochs ke validation losses: 0.90, 0.72, 0.61, 0.55, 0.52, 0.53, 0.50, 0.51, 0.52, 0.54, 0.53, 0.56.

EpochVal lossBest so farBest epochPatience counterAction
10.900.9010Naya best → save
20.720.7220Naya best → save
30.610.6130Naya best → save
40.550.5540Naya best → save
50.520.5250Naya best → save
60.530.5251Sudhaar nahi (0.53 ≥ 0.52)
70.500.5070Naya best → save, counter reset
80.510.5071Sudhaar nahi
90.520.5072Sudhaar nahi
100.540.5073Counter = patience → STOP
11, 12—Kabhi train hi nahi hue
  1. Training epoch 10 ke baad rukti hai. Model me abhi epoch 10 ke weights hain (val loss 0.54).
  2. Saved best = epoch 7 (val loss 0.50) → load_state_dict se wapas.

Patience 3 → stop after epoch 10, restore epoch 7 (asli minimum). Patience 1 → epoch 6 pe hi ruk jaata (0.53 > 0.52), restore epoch 5 — jaldi haar maan li, epoch 7 miss. Patience 5 → bhi epoch 7 hi milta (stop after epoch 12), bas 2 extra epochs ka kharcha.

Ek aur (regularisation worksheet ka check)

Patience 2, validation losses: 0.80, 0.60, 0.62, 0.59, 0.61, 0.63.

  1. Epoch 1: 0.80 best. Epoch 2: 0.60 best. Epoch 3: 0.62 → counter 1.
  2. Epoch 4: 0.59 < 0.60 → naya best, counter 0.
  3. Epoch 5: 0.61 → counter 1. Epoch 6: 0.63 → counter 2 = patience → stop.

Stops after epoch 6, restores epoch 4 (0.59).

Interactive worksheet ka chhota table (train loss, val loss): epoch 1 (0.90, 0.95), 2 (0.70, 0.72), 3 (0.55, 0.58), 4 (0.43, 0.50) ← best validation, 5 (0.35, 0.56), 6 (0.29, 0.64). Epoch 4 se 6 tak training loss girta raha, validation badhta raha — "lower training loss does not always mean better model". Checkpoint: epoch 4.

Hamesha best weights restore karo

Jab training rukti hai, model me aakhri epoch ke weights hote hain, best wale nahi (upar: epoch 10 ka 0.54, na ki epoch 7 ka 0.50). Saved weights wapas daalne padte hain. Keras me EarlyStopping(monitor="val_loss", patience=20, restore_best_weights=True) — dhyaan do, restore_best_weights ka default False hai (slide: Keras implementation me BEST_WEIGHT save karne ka option hai). PyTorch me koi built-in nahi; khud likhte hain:

PyTorch · early stopping loop (worksheet + Lab 14 style)

import copy
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.optim as optim
# X_tr, y_tr, X_va, y_va aur make_mlp() 18.10 wale demo se

torch.manual_seed(0)
model = make_mlp([256, 256, 256, 256])        # wahi bada model jo overfit karta hai
criterion = nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss()
optimizer = optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=0.003)

best_val_loss = float('inf')   # ab tak ka sabse kam val loss
best_state = None              # us waqt ke weights ki photocopy
best_epoch = 0
patience = 20                  # kitne epoch bina sudhaar ke bardaasht karenge
wait = 0                       # patience counter

for epoch in range(1, 401):
    model.train()
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    loss = criterion(model(X_tr), y_tr)
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()

    model.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        val_loss = criterion(model(X_va), y_va).item()

    if val_loss < best_val_loss:          # naya record?
        best_val_loss = val_loss
        best_epoch = epoch
        best_state = copy.deepcopy(model.state_dict())   # weights save
        wait = 0                          # counter reset
    else:
        wait += 1                         # ek aur bekaar epoch
        if wait >= patience:
            print(f"Stopping at epoch {epoch}: no improvement for {patience} epochs")
            break

model.load_state_dict(best_state)         # best weights wapas daalo
model.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    val_loss = criterion(model(X_va), y_va).item()
    val_acc = ((model(X_va) > 0).float() == y_va).float().mean().item()
print(f"Restored epoch {best_epoch} | val loss {val_loss:.4f} | val acc {val_acc:.3f}")

Output

Stopping at epoch 50: no improvement for 20 epochs
Restored epoch 30 | val loss 0.2562 | val acc 0.912
  • Wahi 198,401-param model jo 400 epochs pe val loss 1.6270 tak bigad gaya tha — early stopping ke saath val loss 0.2562, val accuracy 0.912, aur 350 epochs ka compute bhi bacha.
  • model.state_dict() = ek ordered dictionary: har layer ka naam → uska weight/bias tensor (aur BatchNorm ke running stats bhi).
  • copy.deepcopy(...) zaroori hai: state_dict() live tensors ke references deta hai; bina deepcopy ke "saved" copy bhi aage ki training ke saath badalti rahegi aur aakhir me best ki jagah last weights milenge.
  • model.load_state_dict(best_state) = saved weights wapas model me copy.
  • Lab 14 ka fit() yahi karta hai, bas validation accuracy track karke (if val_acc > best_accuracy), aur end me model.load_state_dict(best_state). Loss track karo to "<" (kam behtar), accuracy track karo to ">" (zyada behtar).

Early stopping regularization kyun hai?

  • Weights chhote shuru hote hain (initialization) aur training ke saath dheere-dheere badhte hain. Kam steps = kam badhne ka mauka = chhote weights. Isliye early stopping ka kaam L2 jaisa hi hai. Worksheet: "For a linear net with quadratic error, early stopping is roughly ridge with λ related to 1/(training time)."
  • Pattern pehle, noise baad me: shuru me loss ki sabse badi kami bade, saaf pattern se aati hai jo jaldi seekh liya jaata hai. Noise ek-ek point karke, dheere seekha jaata hai. Jaldi rukne se pattern zyada, noise kam.
  • Effective capacity: training time bhi capacity hai ("time is capacity"). Early stopping is time ko kaat ke effective capacity ghatata hai — "deletes training time". Regularisation worksheet ka jawab: early stopping regularise karta hai kyunki "the optimiser has not finished interpolating noise".
  • Gradient descent quadratic pe small-eigenvalue directions me sabse dheere chalta hai — wahi directions jinhe ridge sabse zyada dabata hai. Unke "khatam" hone se pehle rukna = unhe shrunk chhod dena.

Pros (slide)

Bahut simple. Lagbhag free (validation pe ek forward pass per epoch). "Highly recommended to use for all training along with other techniques" — safety net. Compute bhi bachata hai.

Cons (slide)

"May not work so well if the test set accuracy inflection point is low enough." Validation set ab model choose karne me use ho gaya, to final score ke liye alag test set chahiye. Noisy val loss → patience tune karni padti hai. (Epoch-wise double descent me pehle minimum pe ruk sakta hai.)

Exam Radar

  • Monitor validation loss/accuracy each epoch; stop when no improvement for patience epochs; restore best weights.
  • t* = arg mint Lval(θt) (lab: epoch 80; worksheet: epoch 7 with patience 3).
  • Patience too small → stops too early (noise). Too large → wasted epochs (but same best if restore on).
  • Keras restore_best_weights default = False. PyTorch: manual with copy.deepcopy(model.state_dict()) + load_state_dict.
  • Early stopping ≈ L2 (limits weight growth / effective capacity); "deletes training time".
  • Never use test set to pick the stopping epoch.

Galti mat karna

  • best_state = model.state_dict() (bina deepcopy) — classic bug.
  • Stop ke baad restore bhool jaana → last (kharab) weights ship ho jaate hain.
  • Training loss pe early stopping — bekaar, wo to girta hi rahega.

Dimaag me aise baitha lo

Chai chakhte raho; 3 baar lagatar behtar na ho to gas band, aur best wali chai ki photocopy paroso.

19.8 Data Augmentation aur baaki regularizers

Kahani

Chhote bhai ko "billi" pehchaanna sikhana hai, lekin ghar me billi ki sirf 5 photos hain. Tum smart ho: wahi photo thodi ghuma ke dikhate ho, thodi zoom karke, mirror me ulti karke, thodi left khiska ke. Ab 5 photos se 50 "nayi" photos ban gayi, aur bhai seekh gaya ki billi ulti ho ya tedhi, billi hi hai. Usne kisi ek photo ki detail (jaise "billi hamesha left me baithti hai") ratt nahi li.

Worksheet: "More data: the best regulariser of all." Asli naya data mehenga hai, isliye data augmentation — existing training images pe label-preserving random transformations lagao, taaki model ko har epoch thoda alag version dikhe. Ye effective dataset size badhata hai aur model ko invariances (rotation, shift, flip) sikhata hai. Course slide: regularization ka doosra type = "Data augmentation: increase the size of training data" (slide "Increase the data").

PyTorch · torchvision transforms for augmentation (Labs 12–14 style)

import torch
from torchvision import transforms
from PIL import Image
import numpy as np

# Training ke liye: random badlaav (har epoch naya version)
train_transform = transforms.Compose([
    transforms.RandomHorizontalFlip(p=0.5),          # 50% chance left-right flip
    transforms.RandomRotation(degrees=10),           # -10 se +10 degree random ghumao
    transforms.RandomAffine(degrees=8, translate=(0.08, 0.08), scale=(0.95, 1.05)),
    transforms.ToTensor(),                           # PIL (H, W) 0-255 -> tensor (C, H, W) 0-1
    transforms.Normalize((0.5,), (0.5,)),            # [0, 1] -> [-1, 1]
])

# Validation/test ke liye: koi randomness nahi
eval_transform = transforms.Compose([
    transforms.ToTensor(),
    transforms.Normalize((0.5,), (0.5,)),
])

img = Image.fromarray(np.random.default_rng(0).integers(0, 256, (28, 28), dtype=np.uint8))  # dummy 28x28 grayscale
torch.manual_seed(0)
a = train_transform(img)
b = train_transform(img)
c = eval_transform(img)
print(a.shape, c.shape)
print("two augmented copies equal?", torch.equal(a, b))
print("eval twice equal?", torch.equal(eval_transform(img), c))
print("range:", round(c.min().item(), 3), round(c.max().item(), 3))

Output

torch.Size([1, 28, 28]) torch.Size([1, 28, 28])
two augmented copies equal? False
eval twice equal? True
range: -1.0 1.0
  • transforms.Compose([...]) — transforms ki list ko order me ek ke baad ek lagata hai.
  • RandomHorizontalFlip(p=0.5) — probability p se image left-right mirror. Default p = 0.5.
  • RandomRotation(degrees=10) — [−10°, +10°] me se random angle.
  • RandomAffine(degrees, translate=(a, b), scale=(lo, hi)) — rotation + shift (width ka a fraction, height ka b fraction tak) + zoom ek saath. Lab 14 KMNIST: degrees=8, translate=(0.08, 0.08), scale=(0.95, 1.05); SVHN: degrees=6, translate=(0.06, 0.06).
  • ToTensor() — PIL/numpy (H, W, C) uint8 0–255 → float tensor (C, H, W) 0–1. Normalize(mean, std) — (x − mean)/std per channel; (0.5, 0.5) se [0,1] → [−1,1]. RGB ke liye 3-value tuples: Normalize((0.5, 0.5, 0.5), (0.5, 0.5, 0.5)).
  • Output: same image do baar train_transform se → alag tensors (randomness); eval_transform deterministic.
  • Dataset me lagao: datasets.FashionMNIST(root="data", train=True, download=True, transform=train_transform) (CNN chapter me detail — Chapter 23).

Galti mat karna

  • Augmentation sirf training pe. Validation/test transform me randomness nahi (Lab 14 ka test: "Evaluation transform must not be random").
  • Label-preserving hona chahiye: digits (SVHN, MNIST) ko horizontal flip mat karo — mirror kiya "2" ya "7" asli digit nahi rehta. Lab 14 SVHN: "Do not use horizontal flips; mirrored digits are not label-preserving." Billi ki photo flip karo — theek; "6" ko 180° ghumao to "9" ban jaata hai — galat!

Baaki regularizers ek nazar me

  • Ensembles / Bagging (slides): data ke alag-alag subsets pe kai models train karo (har ek aksar overfit), unka average lo → final model ka variance kam. Neural nets ke liye bagging computationally mehenga — dropout isi ka sasta roop hai (ek network me exponentially many thinned networks, shared weights).
  • Dropout: training me random neurons band, inverted scaling 1/(1 − p); test pe sab on — Chapter 20.
  • Batch normalization: mainly training fast/stable karta hai; minibatch statistics ka noise mild regularization deta hai — Chapter 20.
  • Label smoothing: model ko 100% sure hone se roko (target 1.0 ki jagah, maan lo, 0.9).
  • Noise injection: inputs ya weights me thoda noise (slide reference: "train neural networks with noise to reduce overfitting").

Regularisation worksheet ka one-line map: L1 deletes weights. L2 shrinks weights. Dropout deletes activations (at train). BN re-scales activations. Early stopping deletes training time.

Dimaag me aise baitha lo

Data kam ho to photo ko ghumao-khiskao-zoom karo — lekin "6" ko "9" mat banao.

19.9 Lab 9 — overfit MyNN ko regularize karo (aur sab kuch ek saath)

Lab 9 ka setup: Fashion-MNIST (CSV, 60,000 rows × 785 columns: label + 784 pixels), 80/20 split, pixels /255, batch 32. Baseline MyNN (784 → 128 → 64 → 10) overfit karta hai: ~98% train vs ~89% test. Phir "keep everything the same" (same widths, lr = 0.1, 100 epochs, same loop) aur sirf regularization badlo: har Linear ke baad nn.BatchNorm1d, har ReLU ke baad nn.Dropout(0.3), aur optimizer me weight_decay=1e-4.

PyTorch · Lab 9 · baseline vs regularized MyNN

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.optim as optim

# ---------- Step 1: baseline (no regularization) ----------
class MyNN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, num_features):
        super().__init__()
        self.model = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(num_features, 128),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(128, 64),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(64, 10)                  # 10 classes ke raw logits
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.model(x)

# ---------- Step 2: SAME class + BatchNorm + Dropout ----------
class MyNNReg(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, num_features):
        super().__init__()
        self.model = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(num_features, 128),
            nn.BatchNorm1d(128),               # BatchNorm (Chapter 20)
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Dropout(0.3),                   # Dropout (Chapter 20)
            nn.Linear(128, 64),
            nn.BatchNorm1d(64),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Dropout(0.3),
            nn.Linear(64, 10)
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.model(x)

learning_rate = 0.1
epochs = 100
model = MyNNReg(784).to(device)
criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
optimizer = optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=learning_rate, weight_decay=1e-4)   # L2

for epoch in range(epochs):
    model.train()                      # Dropout ON, BatchNorm batch-stats use/update
    total_epoch_loss = 0
    for batch_features, batch_labels in train_loader:
        batch_features, batch_labels = batch_features.to(device), batch_labels.to(device)
        outputs = model(batch_features)
        loss = criterion(outputs, batch_labels)
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
        total_epoch_loss += loss.item()
    if (epoch + 1) % 10 == 0:
        print(f'Epoch: {epoch + 1} , Loss: {total_epoch_loss/len(train_loader):.4f}')

model.eval()                           # Dropout OFF, BatchNorm running stats
correct, total = 0, 0
with torch.no_grad():
    for batch_features, batch_labels in test_loader:
        batch_features, batch_labels = batch_features.to(device), batch_labels.to(device)
        _, predicted = torch.max(model(batch_features), 1)   # har row ka max-logit class
        total += batch_labels.shape[0]
        correct += (predicted == batch_labels).sum().item()
print(f'test: {correct/total:.4f}')

Output (Lab 9 notebook ke asli logs)

Baseline (no regularization):
Epoch: 10 , Loss: 0.2747     ...     Epoch: 100 , Loss: 0.0621
train: 0.9825 , test: 0.8898          <- gap ≈ 0.093 (overfit)

Regularized (BN + Dropout 0.3 + weight_decay 1e-4):
Epoch: 10 , Loss: 0.3660     ...     Epoch: 100 , Loss: 0.2592
  • Regularized model ka training loss zyada (0.2592 vs 0.0621) — expected: dropout training me neurons band rakhta hai aur weight decay weights ko rokta hai. Ratta mushkil ho gaya — yahi to chahiye tha.
  • Lab ka takeaway: train accuracy thodi girti hai, test accuracy tikti hai → train–test gap chhota. "A smaller train-test gap means the model generalizes better — that is what regularization buys us."
  • Note: lab notebook me regularized model ke accuracy cell ka printed output baseline jaisa hi (0.9825 / 0.8898) dikh raha hai — wo copy hua output lagta hai (aur agle cell me NameError bhi hai). Khud run karke apne numbers dekhna.
  • model.train() / model.eval() yahan zaroori hain kyunki Dropout aur BatchNorm train/eval me alag behave karte hain.
  • torch.max(outputs, 1) → (max values, indices); index = predicted class. outputs.argmax(dim=1) same kaam.

Ek page comparison (worksheet 09, 6.4)

L2L1Early stoppingDropout

Practitioner ka recipe (worksheet 09, 6.2)

  1. Pehle aisa model banao jo training data fit kar sake (overfit bhi kar sake). Agar training data hi fit nahi hota, regularization se kuch nahi hoga.
  2. Early stopping + best-weight restore as a safety net.
  3. Ek add karo: L2 (AdamW ke saath) ya dropout. Log scale pe tune karo, coarse phir fine.
  4. Har change ke baad curves aur gap dobara padho.
  5. Test score ek baar, bilkul end me.

Worksheet Lab 6 ke rough numbers (train acc / val loss / val acc): nothing 100 / 1.59 / 80; patience 50 only 88 / 0.47 / 85; dropout 0.5 only 88 / 0.78 / 87; L2 0.03 + dropout 0.5 → 80 / 0.53 / 77 (underfitting — do regularizers ne zyada dabaa diya). Defaults by architecture (regularisation worksheet): residual conv net → batch norm on, weight decay ~1e-4, early stopping, dropout sirf agar ab bhi overfit; linear model with correlated features → lasso / elastic net; transformer → LayerNorm, residual dropout, weight decay, early stopping.

Exam Radar

  • Lab 9: nn.BatchNorm1d after Linear, nn.Dropout(0.3) after ReLU, optim.SGD(..., lr=0.1, weight_decay=1e-4).
  • Baseline gap: 0.9825 train vs 0.8898 test.
  • Regularized model's training loss is higher — normal.
  • Regularization goal = smaller generalization gap, not lower training loss.

Dimaag me aise baitha lo

Pehle model ko taakat do (fit kare), phir lagaam do (generalize kare) — aur lagaam ek-ek karke kaso.

Chapter 20

Dropout aur Batch Normalization — neurons ki chhutti, marks ka scaling

Co-adaptation · Dropout mask · Inverted dropout (1/(1−p)) · Ensemble of thinned networks · model.train() / model.eval() · Internal covariate shift · μB, σ²B, γ, β · Running stats · BatchNorm1d / BatchNorm2d · LayerNorm

20.1 Problem kya hai? Neurons ek-doosre ke bharose baith jaate hain

Kahani

Socho tumhari gully cricket team me ek star batsman hai, Raju. Har match me baaki sab sochte hain, "Raju hai na, wo sambhal lega." Koi aur batting practice seriously nahi karta. Jis din Raju bimaar pada, poori team 20 runs pe all-out. Team ek insaan pe depend ho gayi thi.

Ab coach ek naya rule banata hai: har practice session me coach random se kuch players ko bench pe bitha dega. Aaj Raju bench pe, kal Sonu, parso Pinky. Kisi ko pata nahi kal kaun khelega. Result? Har player ko khud batting, bowling, fielding seekhni padti hai, kyunki partner kabhi bhi gayab ho sakta hai. Match ke din (test time) coach poori team utaarta hai, aur ab team zyada strong hai, kyunki har player akele bhi kaam ka hai.

Group project me bhi yahi hota hai: agar pata ho ki kisi bhi din koi bhi member absent ho sakta hai, to har member ko poora project samajhna padta hai. Bas yahi Dropout ka idea hai.

Yaad hai Chapter 18 ka overfitting? Model training data ko ratta maar leta hai, noise tak yaad kar leta hai, aur naye data pe fail ho jaata hai. Chapter 19 me humne iske teen ilaaj dekhe: L2 (bade weights pe fine), L1 (faltu weights ko zero), aur early stopping (ratta shuru hone se pehle ruk jao). Course ki slide me regularization ki definition ye thi:

Definition (lecture slide, Goodfellow)

Regularization is any modification we make to a learning algorithm that is intended to reduce its generalization error but not its training error. Matlab: training pe thoda kam perfect chalega, lekin naye data (test) pe zyada achha chalega.

Overfit model ke andar ek khaas cheez hoti hai. Course ki worksheet (L8 Part 2) kehti hai: training data ke ek noisy point ke around "island" banane ke liye network kai neurons ko milkar ek bahut nazuk, finely-balanced combination banana padta hai. Ek neuron doosre ki galti ko cancel karta hai, doosra teesre ki. Is aapsi nirbharta ko kehte hain co-adaptation. Ye combination training data pe perfect hai, lekin bahut fragile hai: naya data aaya, balance toot gaya.

Definition

Co-adaptation = jab neurons akele koi useful feature nahi seekhte, balki ek-doosre ki quirks (khaas aadaton) pe depend karke sirf group me kaam karte hain. Ye overfitting ka ek bada kaaran hai.

Is chapter me do tools hain:

  • Dropout: training ke time random neurons ko ek step ke liye band kar do, taaki koi kisi pe depend na kar sake (regularization).
  • Batch Normalization (BN): har layer ke andar values ko har mini-batch pe "standard scale" pe le aao, phir network ko khud ka scale/shift seekhne do (mainly training ko fast aur stable banata hai, side me thoda regularization).

Teacher ki notes ka ek-line map yaad rakhna: L1 weights delete karta hai. L2 weights shrink karta hai. Dropout training me activations delete karta hai. BN activations ko re-scale karta hai. Early stopping training time delete karta hai.

20.2 Dropout ka mechanism — har step pe naya random "bench"

Dropout ko Srivastava, Hinton, Krizhevsky, Sutskever aur Salakhutdinov ne paper "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (JMLR, 2014) me formally pesh kiya (Hinton ke group ka pehla version 2012 me aaya tha). Idea bahut simple hai:

  1. Har training step (har mini-batch) pe, ek layer ke har neuron ke liye ek sikka uchhalo.
  2. Probability p se wo neuron drop (output = 0), warna keep.
  3. Agle step pe naya random set drop hoga. Ek hi neuron kabhi on, kabhi off.
  4. Dropped neuron ka us step me agli layer pe koi asar nahi, aur backward pass me usme se gradient bhi nahi guzarta (gradient = 0), to us step me uske incoming weights update nahi hote (plain SGD me; lecture slide: "Dropped neurons are not updated in backward training").
  5. Test time pe: koi dropout nahi. Saare neurons on. (Weights delete nahi hote, sirf us step ke liye activation zero hoti hai.)

Sikka uchhalne ko math me Bernoulli random variable kehte hain: ek variable m jo 1 ya 0 hota hai. Har neuron ka apna m. In sab m ki list ko dropout mask kehte hain.

mi ~ Bernoulli(1 − p)   ·   h̃i = mi · hi  (abhi scaling ke bina)
  • hi = neuron i ka asli output (activation ke baad)
  • mi = mask: 1 matlab "khelega", 0 matlab "bench pe"; 1 aane ki probability (1 − p)
  • p = drop probability (PyTorch ka nn.Dropout(p=0.5) wala p), default 0.5
  • h̃i = dropout ke baad jo value agli layer ko jaati hai

Galti mat karna: p ka matlab har jagah alag hai!

  • PyTorch nn.Dropout(p): p = probability of an element to be zeroed (drop). p=0.3 matlab 30% band, 70% chalu.
  • Course worksheet L8 Part 2: r = dropout rate (drop probability), scale = 1/(1 − r). Ye PyTorch ke p jaisa hi hai.
  • Course ki Regularisation lecture sheet aur original paper (Srivastava et al.): p = keep probability! Wahan formula h̃ = (m ⊙ h)/p likha hai aur "typical keep probability p ≈ 0.5 on hidden units, 0.8–0.9 on inputs".
  • MCQ me hamesha dekho: "probability of dropping" ya "probability of retaining/keeping"? Keep = 1 − drop. Keep probability 0.8 = drop rate 0.2.

20.3 Scaling ki problem aur Inverted Dropout

Kahani (cricket continued)

Practice me aadhe players bench pe hain, to jo 5–6 khel rahe hain wo mil ke ~100 runs banate hain. Match ke din poore 11 utarte hain to ~200 runs. Agar team ne practice ke "100 runs" ko normal maan liya tha, to match ka 200 usko bilkul alag duniya lagega. Coach ka jugaad: practice me jo khel rahe hain unke runs ko double gino (kyunki aadhe hi khel rahe hain). Ab practice ka "scaled" score bhi ~200, match ka bhi ~200. Dono duniya same scale pe.

Yahi problem neurons me hai. Agli layer apne input ka ek typical size seekh leti hai. Agar training me aadhe neurons off hain to agli layer ko lagbhag aadha signal milta hai, lekin test pe sab on hain to double signal. Train aur test ka mismatch. Ilaaj: training ke time bache hue (kept) neurons ko 1/(1 − p) se multiply karo. Isko inverted dropout kehte hain, aur PyTorch exactly yahi karta hai.

Training:  h̃i = mi · hi1 − p      Test:  h̃i = hi (kuch nahi badla)
  • p = drop probability (PyTorch), to (1 − p) = keep probability
  • mi ∈ {0, 1}, P(mi = 1) = 1 − p
  • 1/(1 − p) = scale factor: p = 0.5 → ×2; p = 0.2 → ×1.25; p = 0.25 → ×1.3333; p = 0.3 → ×1.4286
  • Kyun 1/(1 − p)? Taaki expected value (average) training me bhi utni hi rahe jitni test pe: E[h̃i] = (1 − p) · hi1 − p + p · 0 = hi

Chalo numbers se samjhein

Sawaal: Ek hidden layer ke 4 neurons ke activations hain h = [2, 4, 6, 8]. Dropout p = 0.5. Is step ka random mask nikla m = [1, 0, 1, 0]. Inverted dropout ke baad output kya hoga? Aur expected value check karo.

  1. Scale factor: 1/(1 − p) = 1/(1 − 0.5) = 1/0.5 = 2
  2. Mask lagao (element-wise multiply): m ⊙ h = [1×2, 0×4, 1×6, 0×8] = [2, 0, 6, 0]
  3. Survivors ko scale karo: [2×2, 0×2, 6×2, 0×2] = [4, 0, 12, 0]
  4. Is ek step ka sum: 4 + 0 + 12 + 0 = 16, jabki asli sum 2 + 4 + 6 + 8 = 20. Ek step me barabar nahi! Dropout noisy hai, aur yahi noise regularization karta hai.
  5. Expected value, neuron 1 ke liye: E[h̃₁] = P(keep) × (2/0.5) + P(drop) × 0 = 0.5 × 4 + 0.5 × 0 = 2 = asli h1. Neuron 4: 0.5 × 16 + 0.5 × 0 = 8. Har neuron ke liye average = asli value.
  6. Python se check kiya: p = 0.5 pe saare 24 = 16 possible masks barabar probable hain; un 16 outputs ka average exactly [2, 4, 6, 8] aata hai.

Jawab: is step ka output [4, 0, 12, 0]; average over masks = [2, 4, 6, 8] = test-time output. Train aur test "on average" match.

Teacher ki board calculation (Regularisation sheet, keep prob 0.5)

Wahan h = (1.2, −0.4, 2.0, 0.8), mask m = (1, 0, 1, 0), aur formula h̃ = m h/p jahan p = keep probability = 0.5.

  1. Unit 1: (1)(1.2)/0.5 = 2.4
  2. Unit 2: (0)(−0.4)/0.5 = 0
  3. Unit 3: (1)(2.0)/0.5 = 4.0
  4. Unit 4: (0)(0.8)/0.5 = 0

Jawab: (2.4, 0, 4.0, 0). "Kept units double." Test pe wahi layer (1.2, −0.4, 2.0, 0.8) aage bhejegi, bina mask, bina 1/p.

Ek aur worksheet sawaal: dropout rate 0.25, kept neuron ka output 2.0 → training me 2.0 / (1 − 0.25) = 2.0 / 0.75 = 2.6667 (option 2.67). Dropped hota to 0.

Ab PyTorch me dekho. nn.Dropout(p=0.5, inplace=False) ek layer (module) hai. Arguments: p = har element ke zero hone ki probability (default 0.5, range 0 se 1); inplace = True karoge to input tensor ko hi badal dega (memory bachti hai, default False). Training mode me ye mask lagata hai aur survivors ko 1/(1 − p) se multiply karta hai; eval mode me input ko jaisa ka taisa lauta deta hai.

PyTorch · nn.Dropout train vs eval

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

torch.manual_seed(25)
drop = nn.Dropout(p=0.5)          # p = DROP hone ki probability
x = torch.tensor([2.0, 4.0, 6.0, 8.0])

drop.train()                      # training mode (naya module default me train mode me hi hota hai)
print("train  :", drop(x))        # mask lagega, survivors x 2
print("train  :", drop(x))        # dobara chalao -> NAYA random mask

drop.eval()                       # evaluation / test mode
print("eval   :", drop(x))        # koi dropout nahi, koi scaling nahi

Output

train  : tensor([ 4.,  0., 12.,  0.])
train  : tensor([ 0.,  8.,  0., 16.])
eval   : tensor([2., 4., 6., 8.])

Dekho: pehli call me exactly hamara worked example aaya (mask [1, 0, 1, 0] → [4, 0, 12, 0]). Doosri call me naya mask [0, 1, 0, 1] → [0, 8, 0, 16]. Survivors hamesha ×2 hain. Eval me input bilkul same.

PyTorch · expected value ka proof, 10 lakh neurons pe

import torch
torch.manual_seed(1)
drop = torch.nn.Dropout(p=0.3)
x = torch.ones(1_000_000)                      # 10 lakh neurons, sab ka output 1
y = drop(x)                                    # train mode
print("zero fraction :", (y == 0).float().mean().item())   # ~0.3 drop hue
print("survivor value:", y[y != 0][0].item())  # 1/(1-0.3) = 1.4286
print("mean of output:", y.mean().item())     # ~1.0 = input ka mean, scaling ka kamaal

Output

zero fraction : 0.30008599162101746
survivor value: 1.4285714626312256
mean of output: 0.9998772740364075

20.4 Purana tareeka: test time pe weights ko (1 − p) se scale karo

Original paper me scaling test time pe hoti thi, training pe nahi. Isko "standard" (non-inverted) dropout kehte hain:

  • Training: sirf mask lagao, koi scaling nahi: h̃ = m ⊙ h.
  • Test: sab neurons on, lekin har output (ya equivalently, us layer ke outgoing weights) ko keep probability (1 − p) se multiply karo: Wtest = (1 − p) · W.

Same example, purane tareeke se

  1. Training (mask [1, 0, 1, 0], no scaling): [2, 0, 6, 0]; expected value per neuron = 0.5 × h = [1, 2, 3, 4]
  2. Test (sab on, × (1 − p) = × 0.5): [2, 4, 6, 8] × 0.5 = [1, 2, 3, 4]

Training ka average [1, 2, 3, 4] aur test [1, 2, 3, 4]: match. Bas scaling "doosri taraf" shift ho gayi.

Inverted dropout (PyTorch, Keras)Standard / original dropout
Trainingmask, phir ÷ (1 − p) (survivors bade)sirf mask
Testkuch nahi, plain forward passoutputs/weights × (1 − p)
Expected value match?HaanHaan
FaydaDeployment code ko dropout ke baare me kuch pata hone ki zaroorat nahiPaper ka original formulation
Inverted isliye popular: test/inference code simple rehta hai. Model ko eval() karo, bas.

20.5 Dropout kaam kyun karta hai? Teen kaaran

Kaaran 1: Co-adaptation khatam (koi partner pe bharosa nahi)

Kisi bhi step pe koi bhi partner gayab ho sakta hai, isliye har neuron ko aisa feature seekhna padta hai jo akele bhi useful ho. "Main tumhari galti cancel karunga, tum meri" wale nazuk combinations reliable nahi rehte, to model unpe depend karna chhod deta hai. Worksheet ka sawaal: "Do hidden units jo sirf cancelling pair ki tarah kaam karte hain, dropout training ke baad?" Jawab: discouraged (reinforce nahi, aur weights exactly zero bhi nahi hote).

Kaaran 2: Ek network me hazaaron networks ka ensemble

Ensemble (bagging) yaad karo: kai alag models train karo aur unka average lo; har model ki alag galtiyan average me cancel ho jaati hain, variance kam hota hai. Lekin neural networks ke liye 100 alag networks train karna bahut mehenga hai (lecture slide: "computationally prohibitive"). Dropout sasta jugaad hai: har mask ek alag chhota network ("thinned network") banata hai, aur sab thinned networks same weights share karte hain. n neurons hon to 2n possible masks: 3 neurons → 2³ = 8 networks, 100 neurons → 2100 networks. Test pe poora network chalana in sab ka (approximately) average lene jaisa hai.

Teacher ka ensemble example (Worksheet L8 Part 2, Fig 5.5)

Do neurons output ko 1 aur 3 contribute karte hain (yani bina dropout output = 1 + 3 = 4). Drop rate r = 0.5, to scale = 2. Chaar possible masks, har ek ki probability 0.25:

MaskCalculationOutput
dono on [1, 1]2 × (1 + 3)8
sirf pehla [1, 0]2 × 12
sirf doosra [0, 1]2 × 36
dono off [0, 0]00
  1. Average: (8 + 2 + 6 + 0) / 4 = 16 / 4 = 4
  2. Test-time full network: 1 + 3 = 4

Jawab: 4 = 4. Saare thinned networks ka average exactly full network ke barabar. Ye linear layer ke liye exact hai; activation (non-linearity) aane pe sirf approximate rehta hai.

Bagging (normal ensemble)

Har model alag train hota hai, alag data subset pe, alag parameters. Prediction: sab models chalao aur average karo. Mehenga.

Dropout

Sab sub-networks ek saath implicitly train hote hain, parameters shared. Prediction: ek hi full network chalao (sab units on) jo average jaisa kaam karta hai. Sasta.

Kaaran 3: Noise injection

Lecture slide: "Each hidden unit is multiplied by a random value at each step of training → adds noise to the training process". Har step pe hidden features me random noise aata hai, to model ko aisi cheezein seekhni padti hain jo noise ke bawajood sahi rahein. Ye ek tarah ka hidden-layer data augmentation hai. (BN bhi batch statistics ki wajah se aisa thoda noise daalta hai, wo aage dekhenge.)

MC Dropout: test pe bhi dropout chalu rakh ke kai predictions ka spread dekho = sasta uncertainty estimate. Default practice nahi hai.

20.6 Dropout kahan lagayein aur p kitna rakhein?

  • Fully-connected (Linear) layers me, activation ke baad: Linear → ReLU → Dropout. Lab 9 aur Lab 12/13 dono yahi pattern use karte hain.
  • Output layer pe nahi: final Linear ke baad dropout lagaoge to class scores (logits) hi random zero ho jayenge.
  • Typical rates (course worksheet): hidden layers pe 0.2 se 0.5, input pe 0 se 0.2. Keep-probability ki language me: hidden 0.5–0.8, input 0.8–0.9. p = 0.5 hidden layers ka classic choice hai (aur PyTorch default).
  • Conv layers me dropout kam rakho ya bilkul nahi (conv layers ke paas parameters kam hote hain aur BN already regularize karta hai). CNN me dropout aksar classifier part me hota hai: Lab 14 me Flatten → Dropout → Linear.
  • Agar conv feature maps pe dropout chahiye to nn.Dropout2d(p): ye single pixels nahi, poora channel (feature map) zero karta hai, kyunki ek channel ke neighbouring pixels highly correlated hote hain; ek-ek pixel drop karne se kuch khaas farak nahi padta.
  • Chhota network + dropout = underfitting. Worksheet ka lab: 4·4 width wala network r = 0.5 pe underfit karta hai, uske paas spare neurons hi nahi. Dropout un networks me lagao jo overfit karne layak bade hain.
Course labDropout kahanValue
Lab 9 (Fashion-MNIST MLP)har ReLU ke baad0.3
Lab 12 (Fashion-MNIST CNN), Lab 13 (CIFAR-10)classifier me har ReLU ke baad0.4 (Lab 13 Optuna range 0.20–0.55, best ≈ 0.27)
Lab 14 KMNIST CNNFlatten ke baad, final Linear se pehle0.30 default, Optuna 0.1–0.5
Lab 14 SVHN ResNetFlatten ke baad0.20 default, Optuna 0.05–0.40

PyTorch · nn.Dropout2d poore channel band karta hai

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

torch.manual_seed(3)
drop2d = nn.Dropout2d(p=0.5)                 # channel-wise dropout
x = torch.ones(1, 4, 2, 2)                   # (N=1, C=4, H=2, W=2)
y = drop2d(x)                                # train mode
for c in range(4):
    print(f"channel {c}:", y[0, c].flatten().tolist())

Output

channel 0: [2.0, 2.0, 2.0, 2.0]
channel 1: [2.0, 2.0, 2.0, 2.0]
channel 2: [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0]
channel 3: [2.0, 2.0, 2.0, 2.0]

Channel 2 ke saare 4 pixels ek saath zero; baaki channels poore ke poore ×2. Input shape (N, C, H, W) chahiye.

20.7 Dropout ki keemat (costs aur surprises)

  • Slower convergence: har step pe sirf ek thinned network ki training hoti hai, to zyada epochs chahiye.
  • Noisy loss curve: har step ka mask alag, to training loss upar-neeche jhoolta hai; decision boundary bhi training ke dauran "jitter" karti hai, end me smooth settle hoti hai.
  • Surprise: dropout ke saath training loss validation loss se UPAR ho sakta hai. Bug nahi hai! Training loss neurons band karke naapa jaata hai, validation poore network (eval mode) se. Lab 9 me bhi regularized model ka training loss (0.2592 at epoch 100) baseline (0.0621) se kaafi upar tha.
  • Ek aur hyperparameter (p) tune karna padta hai, validation set pe (test pe kabhi nahi).
  • Worksheet ka lab: r = 0.5 wide network pe sabse achhi validation accuracy; r = 0.7 training points tak fit nahi kar paaya (underfit). Aur L2 0.03 + dropout 0.5 dono ek saath lagaya to underfit: "One well-chosen method beats two."

20.8 model.train() vs model.eval() — sabse zaroori line

Kahani

Practice me coach players ko bench pe bithata hai, theek hai. Lekin agar coach final match me bhi aadhi team bench pe bitha de, to team haar jayegi aur har baar alag result aayega. Practice mode aur match mode ka switch yaad rakhna coach ki zimmedari hai. PyTorch me ye switch tum ho: model.train() aur model.eval().

Har nn.Module ke paas ek boolean flag hota hai: self.training. Naya model banate hi ye True hota hai.

  • model.train(): training = True (model aur uske saare sub-modules me). Dropout ON (mask + scale), BatchNorm batch ke stats use karta hai aur running stats update karta hai.
  • model.eval(): training = False. Dropout OFF (identity), BatchNorm saved running stats use karta hai.
  • model.eval() gradients band nahi karta! Uske liye alag se with torch.no_grad(): lagao (memory aur speed ke liye). Dono alag kaam hain.

PyTorch · same input, dono modes

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class DropNet(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, p=0.5):
        super().__init__()
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(4, 8)
        self.drop = nn.Dropout(p=p)     # module wala dropout
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(8, 1)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = F.relu(self.fc1(x))         # (N, 4) -> (N, 8)
        x = self.drop(x)                # train me zero+scale, eval me kuch nahi
        return self.fc2(x)              # (N, 8) -> (N, 1)

torch.manual_seed(42)
model = DropNet(p=0.5)
x = torch.tensor([[1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0]])   # ek hi sample, shape (1, 4)

model.train()
print("train mode:", [round(model(x).item(), 4) for _ in range(3)])

model.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    print("eval  mode:", [round(model(x).item(), 4) for _ in range(3)])
print("model.training =", model.training)

Output

train mode: [0.1854, 1.5576, 1.1825]
eval  mode: [0.9575, 0.9575, 0.9575]
model.training = False

Same input, train mode me har baar alag jawab (random mask). Eval mode me hamesha same, deterministic jawab. Agar evaluation se pehle model.eval() bhool gaye to test accuracy random aur kam aayegi.

Functional dropout: F.dropout

F.dropout(input, p=0.5, training=True, inplace=False) ek function hai, module nahi. Iska training argument default me True hai, aur ye model ka mode apne aap nahi dekhta. Isliye forward ke andar hamesha training=self.training pass karo.

PyTorch · F.dropout ka sahi aur galat use

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class FuncDropNet(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, p=0.5):
        super().__init__()
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(4, 8)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(8, 1)
        self.p = p

    def forward(self, x):
        x = F.relu(self.fc1(x))
        # SAHI: training flag model ke mode se aata hai (model.train()/eval() isko set karte hain)
        x = F.dropout(x, p=self.p, training=self.training)
        return self.fc2(x)

torch.manual_seed(42)
net = FuncDropNet()
x = torch.tensor([[1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0]])
net.train()
print("train:", round(net(x).item(), 4), round(net(x).item(), 4))   # alag-alag
net.eval()
print("eval :", round(net(x).item(), 4), round(net(x).item(), 4))   # dono baar same

# GALAT: training flag diya hi nahi -> F.dropout ka default training=True
h = torch.ones(6)
torch.manual_seed(3)
print(F.dropout(h, p=0.5))      # model eval me ho tab bhi ye drop karega!

Output

train: 0.1854 1.5576
eval : 0.9575 0.9575
tensor([2., 2., 0., 2., 0., 0.])

Labs ka standard loop pattern (Lab 9, Lab 12–14): har epoch ki shuruaat me model.train(), evaluation se pehle model.eval() + torch.no_grad(). Lab 9 ke comments: "training mode (Dropout on, BatchNorm updates)" aur "evaluation mode (Dropout off, BatchNorm uses running stats)". Evaluate karne ke baad agle epoch me wapas model.train() bhoolna bhi ek common bug hai, isliye loop ke andar har epoch ke start me hi likho.

Lab pattern · training loop skeleton

for epoch in range(epochs):
    model.train()                       # Dropout ON, BN batch-stats + running update
    for xb, yb in train_loader:
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss = criterion(model(xb), yb)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()

    model.eval()                        # Dropout OFF, BN running stats
    with torch.no_grad():               # gradients ki zaroorat nahi
        val_loss = criterion(model(X_val), y_val).item()

Exam Radar · Dropout

  • Paper: Srivastava, Hinton, Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Salakhutdinov, JMLR 2014, "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting".
  • Dropout ek regularization technique hai; sirf training me active; test pe full network.
  • PyTorch nn.Dropout(p=0.5): p = drop probability, default 0.5; training me survivors × 1/(1 − p) (inverted dropout); eval me identity.
  • Scale examples: p = 0.5 → ×2, p = 0.2 → ×1.25, p = 0.25 → ×1.3333, p = 0.3 → ×1.4286, p = 0.4 → ×1.6667.
  • Inverted dropout: scaling training me; standard dropout: test pe weights × (1 − p) (keep prob). Dono me expected value match.
  • Kyun kaam karta hai: co-adaptation rokta hai; 2n thinned networks ka implicit ensemble (weights shared, bagging se alag); noise injection.
  • Typical: hidden 0.2–0.5, input 0–0.2 (keep prob: hidden 0.5–0.8, input 0.8–0.9). Conv me kam / Dropout2d (poore channels).
  • Costs: slow convergence, noisy loss, zyada epochs; training loss > validation loss possible.
  • F.dropout ka training default True; use training=self.training.
  • Dropped neuron ke weights us step me update nahi hote (gradient zero).

Galti mat karna

  • "Dropout weights ko permanently delete karta hai" — galat. Sirf ek step ke liye activation zero; stored weights dense rehte hain (wo L1 hai jo weights zero karta hai).
  • "Test pe bhi dropout lagta hai" — galat (default practice me). Test = full network, no mask, inverted me no scaling.
  • "Inverted dropout me test pe ÷(1 − p) karte hain" — galat. Inverted me scaling sirf training me.
  • Keep probability aur drop probability mix mat karo. PyTorch ka p = drop.
  • Output layer ke baad dropout mat lagao; chhote network pe bhari dropout = underfitting.
  • model.eval() ≠ torch.no_grad(). Pehla layers ka behaviour badalta hai, doosra gradient tracking band karta hai.

Dimaag me aise baitha lo

Practice me random players bench pe, survivors ka score double gino; match me poori team, normal score. Train: mask + ×1/(1−p). Eval: kuch nahi.

20.9 Batch Normalization — motivation: har layer ka "input" hilta rehta hai

Kahani

School me ek scholarship ke liye teen sections ke toppers compare karne hain. Section A ki teacher bahut strict hai: marks 30–60 ke beech. Section B ki teacher dil-khol ke deti hai: 70–100. Section C ka paper out of 50 tha. Ab "75 marks" ka matlab har section me alag hai! Principal kya karta hai? Har section ke marks ko us section ke average aur spread se rescale karta hai: "class average se kitna upar, kitne spread ke units me?" Ab sab ek common scale pe aa gaye, comparison fair.

Lekin principal ye bhi jaanta hai ki scholarship committee ko shayad "out of 100" wala scale pasand hai. To normalize karne ke baad wo apni pasand ka scale (stretch) aur center (shift) laga deta hai. Bas: normalize karo, phir apna scale aur shift seekho. Yahi Batch Normalization hai.

Batch Normalization ko Sergey Ioffe aur Christian Szegedy (Google) ne 2015 me paper "Batch Normalization: Accelerating Deep Network Training by Reducing Internal Covariate Shift" (ICML 2015) me diya.

Original motivation: Internal Covariate Shift (ICS)

Definition (lecture slide)

Internal Covariate Shift: The change in the distribution of network activations due to the change in network parameters during training.

Simple bhasha me: layer 5 apne input (layer 4 ke outputs) pe kaam karna seekh rahi hai. Lekin har step pe layers 1–4 ke weights bhi badal rahe hain, to layer 5 ke inputs ka distribution (mean, spread) hilta rehta hai. Layer 5 ek "moving target" ke peeche bhaag rahi hai; usko baar-baar naye distribution ke hisaab se adapt karna padta hai. Slide ke hisaab se problems: slower training aur bada learning rate use karna mushkil. BN ka jawab: har layer ke inputs ka mean aur variance fix kar do (har mini-batch pe 0 aur 1), to distribution itna nahi hilega.

Baad ki samajh: loss landscape smooth hota hai

2018 me Santurkar et al. ("How Does Batch Normalization Help Optimization?") ne dikhaya ki BN ka asli fayda shayad ICS kam karna nahi, balki loss landscape ko smoother banana hai: gradients zyada predictable aur stable ho jaate hain, isliye bada learning rate safe ho jaata hai aur training fast hoti hai. Teacher ki notes: "Two stories: internal covariate shift (Ioffe & Szegedy) versus a smoother loss (Santurkar et al.). Operationally you need neither to implement the four lines." Exam ke liye dono yaad rakho: paper ka title ICS bolta hai; modern view smoother optimization bolta hai.

20.10 BN algorithm — chaar lines

Ek mini-batch me m samples hain. Ek feature (ek neuron ka output, ya CNN me ek channel) lo. Uski m values: x1, …, xm. BN ye chaar kaam karta hai (har feature ke liye alag-alag):

1) μB = 1m Σi=1..m xi
2) σ²B = 1m Σi=1..m (xi − μB)²
3) x̂i = xi − μB√σ²B + ε
4) yi = γ · x̂i + β
  • m = mini-batch size (kitne samples ek saath aaye)
  • μB = batch mean ("B" = batch). Is feature ka batch me average
  • σ²B = batch variance, biased / population form: divide by m, not m − 1 (teacher: "Use the population variance (divide by N)")
  • ε (epsilon) = chhota number (PyTorch default 1e−5) taaki variance 0 ho to bhi division by zero na ho
  • x̂i = normalized value: ab is feature ka batch me mean 0, variance ≈ 1
  • γ (gamma) = learnable scale (PyTorch me bn.weight, init 1)
  • β (beta) = learnable shift (PyTorch me bn.bias, init 0)
  • yi = BN ka final output, jo agli layer/activation ko jaata hai

Step 3 asal me "z-score" hai: x apne batch ke average se kitne standard deviations door hai. Step 4 network ko azaadi deta hai ki wo apna pasandeeda mean (β) aur spread (γ) khud seekhe. γ aur β backprop se baaki weights ki tarah train hote hain.

20.11 Worked example: batch [2, 4, 6, 8]

Chalo numbers se samjhein

Sawaal: Ek neuron ka output ek mini-batch (m = 4) me x = [2, 4, 6, 8] hai. γ = 2, β = 1, ε = 1e−5. BN output nikalo.

  1. Mean: μ = (2 + 4 + 6 + 8)/4 = 20/4 = 5
  2. Deviations: x − μ = [2−5, 4−5, 6−5, 8−5] = [−3, −1, 1, 3]
  3. Squares: [9, 1, 1, 9], sum = 20
  4. Biased variance: σ² = 20/4 = 5 (agar /3 karte to 6.6667 aata: wo unbiased hai, yahan nahi chahiye)
  5. Denominator: √(5 + 0.00001) = √5.00001 ≈ 2.2361 (ε ke bina √5 = 2.236068; ε ka asar 4 decimals pe nahi dikhta)
  6. Normalize: x̂ = [−3, −1, 1, 3] / 2.2361 ≈ [−1.3416, −0.4472, 0.4472, 1.3416]
  7. Check: x̂ ka mean = 0; x̂ ka variance = (1.8 + 0.2 + 0.2 + 1.8)/4 = 4/4 = 1 (≈ 0.999998 ε ki wajah se)
  8. Scale & shift: y = 2·x̂ + 1
    y₁ = 2(−1.341639) + 1 = −2.683279 + 1 = −1.683279 ≈ −1.6833
    y₂ = 2(−0.447213) + 1 = −0.894426 + 1 = 0.105574 ≈ 0.1056
    y₃ = 2(0.447213) + 1 = 0.894426 + 1 = 1.894426 ≈ 1.8944
    y₄ = 2(1.341639) + 1 = 2.683279 + 1 = 3.683279 ≈ 3.6833

Jawab: y ≈ [−1.6833, 0.1056, 1.8944, 3.6833]. Inka mean = β = 1, std = γ = 2.

Note: teacher ki sheet ne rounded x̂ (1.3416) se 2 × 1.3416 + 1 = 3.6832 likha hai; exact calculation 3.68328 → 3.6833 deta hai. MCQ me −1.683 / 3.683 dono ka matlab same hai.

Teacher ka board example: u = (1, 3, 5, 7), ε = 0, γ = 2, β = 1

  1. μB = 16/4 = 4
  2. σ²B = (9 + 1 + 1 + 9)/4 = 5, √5 ≈ 2.2361
  3. û ≈ (−1.3416, −0.4472, +0.4472, +1.3416)
  4. y = 2û + 1 ≈ (−1.6832, 0.1056, 1.8944, 3.6832)

Dhyan do: (1, 3, 5, 7) aur (2, 4, 6, 8) ka x̂ bilkul same hai! Kyunki saare numbers +1 shift hue, mean bhi +1 shift hua, aur (x − μ) me shift cancel ho gaya. BN kisi bhi constant shift ko mita deta hai. Ye baat 20.15 me "bias=False" samjhayegi.

20.12 γ aur β kyun chahiye? Normalization ko "undo" karne ki azaadi

Agar BN sirf normalize karta (step 3 pe ruk jaata), to har layer ka input hamesha mean 0, variance 1 pe forced rehta. Ye kabhi-kabhi network ki representational power (kya-kya represent kar sakta hai) chheen leta hai. Example: sigmoid ke baad BN... ulta socho, BN ke baad sigmoid. x̂ zyada tar −2 se +2 ke beech hai, jahan sigmoid lagbhag seedhi line jaisa hai. Matlab non-linearity ka fayda hi khatam! γ aur β se network chahe to values ko sigmoid ke curved hisse me bhej sakta hai.

Sabse important property: agar network ko lage ki normalization bekaar hai, to wo γ = √(σ² + ε) aur β = μ seekh ke normalization ko poori tarah undo kar sakta hai:

Undo check

Batch [2, 4, 6, 8]: γ = √(5 + 0.00001) ≈ 2.2361, β = μ = 5 rakho.

  1. y₁ = 2.2361 × (−1.3416) + 5 ≈ −3 + 5 = 2
  2. y₄ = 2.2361 × 1.3416 + 5 ≈ 3 + 5 = 8

Output = [2, 4, 6, 8] = original input (Python se verify kiya). Yaani BN laga ke network ne kuch "khoya" nahi; worst case me wo identity ban sakta hai. Isliye γ, β "restore representational power".

Note: γ aur β per feature hain (har neuron/channel ka apna ek γ aur ek β), poore layer ke liye ek nahi.

20.13 BatchNorm1d vs BatchNorm2d — kis cheez ka average?

  • nn.BatchNorm1d(num_features): MLP (Linear layers) ke liye. Input shape (N, C) (ya (N, C, L) sequences ke liye). Har feature/neuron ka μ aur σ² batch ke N samples ke upar. num_features = C = previous Linear ka out_features.
  • nn.BatchNorm2d(num_features): CNN ke liye. Input (N, C, H, W). Har channel ka μ aur σ² (N, H, W) teeno ke upar: us channel ki saari images ke saare pixels. num_features = C = previous Conv2d ka out_channels. Kyun per-channel? Ek channel = ek filter ka output, jo image me har jagah same kaam karta hai; isliye uske saare positions ko ek hi scale do (Chapter 23 ke CNN aur Chapter 25 ke ResNet me har conv ke baad yahi BatchNorm2d aayega).
  • Dono ke andar: per feature/channel 2 learnable parameters (γ = weight, β = bias) + 2 buffers (running_mean, running_var) + ek counter num_batches_tracked. Buffers training se update hote hain lekin gradient se nahi, isliye "parameters" me count nahi hote (par state_dict me save hote hain).

Shape aur count ka example

Sawaal: 8 images ka batch, 16 channels, 32×32 size. nn.BatchNorm2d(16) kitne numbers se ek channel ka mean nikalta hai? Kitne learnable params?

  1. Ek channel ke values: N × H × W = 8 × 32 × 32 = 8192
  2. Kitne alag (μ, σ²) pairs: C = 16
  3. Learnable params: 16 γ + 16 β = 32; buffers: 16 running_mean + 16 running_var (+ num_batches_tracked)

Jawab: 8192 values per channel, 32 learnable parameters. Output shape input jaisa hi: (8, 16, 32, 32).

PyTorch signature (exam ke liye defaults yaad karo): nn.BatchNorm1d(num_features, eps=1e-05, momentum=0.1, affine=True, track_running_stats=True). affine=True matlab γ, β learnable hain (False karoge to sirf normalize). track_running_stats=True matlab running mean/var maintain karo (eval ke liye). BatchNorm2d ke same arguments hain.

PyTorch · manual BN = nn.BatchNorm1d (train mode)

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

x = torch.tensor([[2.0], [4.0], [6.0], [8.0]])   # (N=4, C=1): 4 samples, 1 feature

bn = nn.BatchNorm1d(num_features=1)              # eps=1e-5, momentum=0.1 default
with torch.no_grad():
    bn.weight.fill_(2.0)                          # gamma = 2
    bn.bias.fill_(1.0)                            # beta  = 1

# ---- manual BN (train mode wala formula) ----
mu = x.mean(dim=0)                                # batch mean, per feature (dim=0 = batch axis)
var = x.var(dim=0, unbiased=False)                # BIASED variance (divide by m)
x_hat = (x - mu) / torch.sqrt(var + 1e-5)
y_manual = 2.0 * x_hat + 1.0

bn.train()
y_torch = bn(x)
print("mu, var :", mu.item(), var.item())
print("x_hat   :", x_hat.flatten())
print("manual  :", y_manual.flatten())
print("nn.BN   :", y_torch.detach().flatten())
print("same?   :", torch.allclose(y_manual, y_torch, atol=1e-6))

Output

mu, var : 5.0 5.0
x_hat   : tensor([-1.3416, -0.4472,  0.4472,  1.3416])
manual  : tensor([-1.6833,  0.1056,  1.8944,  3.6833])
nn.BN   : tensor([-1.6833,  0.1056,  1.8944,  3.6833])

Hamara haath ka hisaab, manual code aur nn.BatchNorm1d: teeno same. unbiased=False bahut zaroori hai; default x.var() unbiased (÷ (m − 1)) hota hai aur match nahi karega.

PyTorch · BatchNorm1d (multi-feature) aur BatchNorm2d

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

torch.manual_seed(0)
# BatchNorm1d: (N, C) -> har column (feature) ka apna mean/var
x = torch.randn(32, 3) * torch.tensor([1.0, 10.0, 100.0]) + torch.tensor([5.0, -20.0, 300.0])
bn1 = nn.BatchNorm1d(3)
y = bn1(x)                                  # naya module train mode me hota hai
print("before mean:", x.mean(0))
print("after  mean:", y.mean(0).detach())
print("after  std :", y.std(0, unbiased=False).detach())
for name, p in bn1.named_parameters():
    print("param ", name, tuple(p.shape))
for name, b in bn1.named_buffers():
    print("buffer", name, tuple(b.shape))

# BatchNorm2d: (N, C, H, W) -> har CHANNEL ka mean/var, (N, H, W) ke upar
imgs = torch.randn(8, 16, 32, 32) * 3 + 7
bn2 = nn.BatchNorm2d(16)
out = bn2(imgs)
print(out.shape)                                             # shape same rehta hai
print("ch-0 mean/std:", round(out[:, 0].mean().item(), 4), round(out[:, 0].std(unbiased=False).item(), 4))
print("values per channel:", 8 * 32 * 32)
print("learnable params:", sum(p.numel() for p in bn2.parameters()))   # 16 gamma + 16 beta
print(bn2)

20.14 Train vs Eval: running mean aur running variance

Kahani

Principal wala marks scaling yaad karo. Wo section ke average se scale karta tha. Lekin ab ek akela naya student admission ke liye aaya, uska koi section nahi, koi "batch" nahi. Uske marks ko kis average se scale karein? Principal ke paas pichhle saalon ka running average likha hua hai: "hamare school me typically average 65, spread 12". Wahi use karo.

Test time pe aksar ek hi image aati hai (batch of 1), ya batches ka composition random hota hai. Agar BN test pe bhi batch stats use kare to ek image ka prediction is baat pe depend karega ki uske saath batch me aur kaun-si images thi! Ye galat hai. Isliye training ke dauran BN har feature ke liye ek running (exponential moving) average rakhta hai, aur model.eval() me wahi use karta hai.

running_mean ← (1 − momentum) · running_mean + momentum · μB
running_var ← (1 − momentum) · running_var + momentum · σ²B, unbiased
Eval:  y = γ · x − running_mean√running_var + ε + β
  • momentum = 0.1 (PyTorch default): naye batch ko 10% weight, purane running value ko 90%. (Chapter 16 ka EWMA yaad karo; yahan βEWMA = 1 − momentum = 0.9.)
  • Shuruaat: running_mean = 0, running_var = 1 (har feature ke liye)
  • σ²B, unbiased = Σ(x − μ)²/(m − 1): running_var me PyTorch unbiased variance daalta hai, jabki training ke normalization me biased (÷ m) use hota hai
  • Eval me batch ka μB, σ²B nahi lagta; har sample alag-alag, deterministic tareeke se normalize hota hai
Dhyan: BN ka "momentum" optimizer wale momentum se ulta hai. Yahan 0.1 = NAYE value ka weight. momentum=None karo to simple cumulative average.

Chalo numbers se samjhein: do batches ke baad running stats

Ek feature, nn.BatchNorm1d(1), γ = 1, β = 0 (defaults). Batch 1 = [2, 4, 6, 8], batch 2 = [1, 3, 5, 7]. Phir eval mode me x = 2, 6, 8 ka output?

  1. Start: running_mean = 0, running_var = 1
  2. Batch 1: μ = 5; unbiased var = 20/(4 − 1) = 6.6667
  3. Update: running_mean = 0.9 × 0 + 0.1 × 5 = 0.5; running_var = 0.9 × 1 + 0.1 × 6.6667 = 0.9 + 0.6667 = 1.5667
  4. Batch 2: μ = 4; deviations [−3, −1, 1, 3], unbiased var = 20/3 = 6.6667
  5. Update: running_mean = 0.9 × 0.5 + 0.1 × 4 = 0.45 + 0.4 = 0.85; running_var = 0.9 × 1.5667 + 0.1 × 6.6667 = 1.41 + 0.6667 = 2.0767
  6. Eval, x = 6: (6 − 0.85)/√(2.0767 + 0.00001) = 5.15/1.4411 = 3.5737
  7. Eval, x = 2: (2 − 0.85)/1.4411 = 1.15/1.4411 = 0.7980; x = 8: 7.15/1.4411 = 4.9616

Jawab: running_mean = 0.85, running_var ≈ 2.0767; eval outputs ≈ [0.7980, 3.5737, 4.9616]. Sirf 2 batches hue hain, isliye running_mean (0.85) abhi data ke asli mean (dono batches ka mean 4.5) se kaafi door hai, kyunki wo 0 se shuru hua tha; hazaaron batches ke baad running stats asli data ke stats ke paas pahunch jaate hain.

PyTorch · running stats ka update aur eval output

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

bn = nn.BatchNorm1d(1)                     # gamma=1, beta=0 (default)
print("start   :", bn.running_mean.item(), bn.running_var.item())   # 0 aur 1 se shuru

bn.train()
bn(torch.tensor([[2.0], [4.0], [6.0], [8.0]]))      # batch 1: mean 5, unbiased var 6.6667
print("batch 1 :", bn.running_mean.item(), round(bn.running_var.item(), 4))

bn(torch.tensor([[1.0], [3.0], [5.0], [7.0]]))      # batch 2: mean 4, unbiased var 6.6667
print("batch 2 :", round(bn.running_mean.item(), 4), round(bn.running_var.item(), 4))
print("batches :", bn.num_batches_tracked.item())

bn.eval()                                  # ab running stats use honge
x_test = torch.tensor([[2.0], [6.0], [8.0]])
with torch.no_grad():
    print("eval out:", bn(x_test).flatten())
manual = (x_test - 0.85) / torch.sqrt(torch.tensor(2.0766667) + 1e-5)
print("manual  :", manual.flatten())

Output

start   : 0.0 1.0
batch 1 : 0.5 1.5667
batch 2 : 0.85 2.0767
batches : 2
eval out: tensor([0.7980, 3.5737, 4.9616])
manual  : tensor([0.7980, 3.5737, 4.9616])

Batch size 1 ka panga

Training me agar batch me sirf 1 sample hai to variance = 0 aur normalized value hamesha 0 (x − μ = 0). Isliye PyTorch train mode me error deta hai. Eval me koi dikkat nahi (running stats).

PyTorch · batch of 1 in train mode

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

bn = nn.BatchNorm1d(4)
one = torch.randn(1, 4)              # batch me sirf 1 sample
bn.train()
try:
    bn(one)
except ValueError as e:
    print("ValueError:", e)
bn.eval()
print(bn(one).shape)                 # eval me chalega: running stats use hote hain

Output

ValueError: Expected more than 1 value per channel when training, got input size torch.Size([1, 4])
torch.Size([1, 4])

Teacher ke MCQs: "Test pe ek image pass karte ho, BN kisse normalize kare?" → running mean aur variance. "BN ko train mode me chhod ke ek-ek image test ki?" → predictions batch-dependent ya degenerate ho jaate hain. (Ek practical tip: DataLoader me drop_last=True se aakhri chhota batch, jo shayad size 1 ka ho, skip ho jaata hai.)

20.15 BN kahan lagayein? Aur bias=False kyun?

  • Original paper aur zyada-tar modern code: Linear/Conv → BN → ReLU. Yaani activation se pehle, pre-activation z = Wx + b ko normalize karo. Lab 9 (Linear → BatchNorm1d → ReLU → Dropout), Lab 14 (Conv2d(bias=False) → BatchNorm2d → ReLU) aur ResNet blocks (Chapter 25) isi order me hain.
  • Lab 12 aur Lab 13 me order hai Conv → ReLU → BatchNorm2d → MaxPool (activation ke baad). Ye bhi practice me chalta hai aur kaam karta hai. Exam me "standard/original placement" pooche to: before the activation.
  • Dropout ke saath: Lab 9 ka order Linear → BN → ReLU → Dropout. Output layer pe na BN na Dropout (raw logits chahiye, CrossEntropyLoss khud softmax lagata hai).

bias=False ka raaz

Linear/Conv ka bias b har sample me same constant jodta hai. BN step 1–3 me mean ghatata hai, aur constant shift mean me bhi aa jaata hai, to cancel: (x + b) − mean(x + b) = x − mean(x). Matlab BN se pehle bias bekaar hai (uska gradient bhi 0 ho jaata hai). BN ka β already "shift" ka kaam karta hai. Isliye bias=False likh ke ek redundant parameter bacha lo (Lab 14 ka note: "Use bias=False for convolutions followed by batch normalization").

PyTorch · constant shift BN ke baad gayab

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

bn = nn.BatchNorm1d(1)
x = torch.tensor([[2.0], [4.0], [6.0], [8.0]])
print(bn(x).detach().flatten())
print(bn(x + 10).detach().flatten())      # +10 bias jaisa shift: output SAME

Output

tensor([-1.3416, -0.4472,  0.4472,  1.3416])
tensor([-1.3416, -0.4472,  0.4472,  1.3416])

PyTorch · Lab 14 style conv-BN-ReLU block

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

def conv_bn_relu(in_c, out_c):
    return nn.Sequential(
        nn.Conv2d(in_c, out_c, kernel_size=3, padding=1, bias=False),  # bias ki zaroorat nahi
        nn.BatchNorm2d(out_c),                                          # beta hi bias ka kaam karega
        nn.ReLU(inplace=True)
    )

block = conv_bn_relu(3, 32)
print(block)
print("params:", sum(p.numel() for p in block.parameters()))
print(block(torch.randn(4, 3, 28, 28)).shape)

Output

Sequential(
  (0): Conv2d(3, 32, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1), bias=False)
  (1): BatchNorm2d(32, eps=1e-05, momentum=0.1, affine=True, bias=True, track_running_stats=True)
  (2): ReLU(inplace=True)

torch.Size([4, 32, 28, 28])

Params: conv weights 32 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 864 + BN 32 γ + 32 β = 64 = 928. Bias hota to 32 aur (bekaar) params.

Lab 9 ka regularized MyNN (BN + Dropout + weight decay)

PyTorch · Lab 9 · Fashion-MNIST MLP with BatchNorm1d + Dropout

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class MyNN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, num_features):
        super().__init__()
        self.model = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(num_features, 128),
            nn.BatchNorm1d(128),     # Linear ke baad, ReLU se pehle (num_features = 128)
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Dropout(0.3),         # activation ke baad
            nn.Linear(128, 64),
            nn.BatchNorm1d(64),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Dropout(0.3),
            nn.Linear(64, 10)        # output layer: na BN, na Dropout (raw logits)
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.model(x)

model = MyNN(784)
print(model)
total = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())
print("trainable params:", total)
bn_params = sum(p.numel() for m in model.modules() if isinstance(m, nn.BatchNorm1d) for p in m.parameters())
print("BN params (gamma+beta):", bn_params)
x = torch.randn(32, 784)                     # (N=32, 784) batch
print(model(x).shape)                        # (32, 10)
# Lab 9 me optimizer: optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.1, weight_decay=1e-4)  -> L2 bhi

    (2): ReLU()
    (3): Dropout(p=0.3, inplace=False)
    (4): Linear(in_features=128, out_features=64, bias=True)
    (5): BatchNorm1d(64, eps=1e-05, momentum=0.1, affine=True, bias=True, track_running_stats=True)
    (6): ReLU()
