Output ko padhna seekho

  • Loss har epoch ghat raha hai (0.65 → 0.17) — seekh raha hai.
  • Test accuracy ~92% (MLP Fashion-MNIST par aam taur par ~88–89% ke aas-paas rukta hai) — CNN ka fayda.
  • Final train 0.9625 vs test 0.9204 → gap 0.0421 = thoda overfitting. Lab ka note: "That gap is overfitting… exactly why we added Dropout, BatchNorm and weight decay." Aur kam karna ho: zyada dropout, data augmentation, early stopping, simpler model.
  • Epoch ke andar wali "Train Acc" (0.9414) final evaluate wali (0.9625) se kam kyun? Training ke dauraan Dropout on tha aur weights beech me badal rahe the; final evaluate eval mode me poore trained model se hai.

Ek nayi photo par prediction

PyTorch · single image predict (Lab 12 style)

img, true_label = test_set[15]              # ek (1, 28, 28) image
x = img.unsqueeze(0).to(device)             # batch dim jodo -> (1, 1, 28, 28)
# (Lab 12 CSV route: torch.tensor(pixels / 255.0).reshape(1, 1, 28, 28))

model.eval()                                # zaroori: Dropout off, BN running stats
with torch.no_grad():
    logits = model(x)                       # (1, 10)
    probs = torch.softmax(logits, dim=1)    # probabilities chahiye to (sum = 1)
    pred = torch.argmax(logits, dim=1).item()

print("Predicted:", train_set.classes[pred], "| Actual:", train_set.classes[true_label])

Lab 12 ke run me index 15 wali photo par output aaya tha: "Model predicted : Sandal / Actual label : Sandal".

Exam Radar

  • Training step order: forward → loss → zero_grad → backward → step (zero_grad ka kaam pichhle batch ke gradients mitaana hai, kyunki PyTorch gradients jodta rehta hai; isliye har backward() se pehle).
  • torch.max(outputs, 1) returns (values, indices); indices = predicted class. outputs.argmax(dim=1) same (Lab 13 style).
  • model.eval() + torch.no_grad() for evaluation; model.train() wapas training se pehle.
  • CrossEntropyLoss: input raw logits (N, 10), target class indices (N,) long. Last layer par softmax mat lagao.
  • Lab 12 hyperparameters: SGD, lr = 0.01, weight_decay = 1e-4, epochs = 12, batch 32, Dropout 0.4. Result ≈ 92% test.
  • Single image ko model me bhejne se pehle batch dim: (1, 1, 28, 28).

Galti mat karna

  • model.eval() bhoolna → Dropout prediction ke time bhi neurons band karega, BN batch stats use karega → galat/random jaisa result.
  • loss.item() ki jagah loss ko list me jodte jaana → graph memory me atka rehta hai.
  • .to(device) sirf model ko karna, data ko nahi (ya ulta) → device mismatch error.

Dimaag me aise baitha lo

"Data → Model → Loss/Optim → Loop (train) → Evaluate (eval + no_grad)". Paanch dabbe, har exam me wahi.

23.22 CIFAR-10 (Lab 13) aur data augmentation

Kahani

Chhote bhai ko "billi" pehchaanna sikhana hai. Agar use sirf ek hi photo dikhao (billi beech me, seedhi khadi), to wo ulti taraf mudi billi ya kone me baithi billi par confuse hoga. Samajhdaar tareeka: wahi billi ko alag-alag tarah dikhao — mirror me, thoda left, thoda right, thoda zoom. Har baar label wahi "billi". Ye hai data augmentation: naya data collect kiye bina, purani photos ke label-preserving naye roop banana.

Lab 13: Fashion-MNIST se CIFAR-10 par kya badla?

PartFashion-MNIST (Lab 12)CIFAR-10 (Lab 13)
Image28×28, 1 channel (grayscale)32×32, 3 channels (RGB)
Input to CNN(batch, 1, 28, 28)(batch, 3, 32, 32)
First convConv2d(1, 32, 3, padding='same')Conv2d(3, 32, 3, padding='same')
Spatial sizes28 → 14 → 732 → 16 → 8
Flatten64 × 7 × 7 = 313664 × 8 × 8 = 4096
Data prepreshape(-1, 1, 28, 28), /255permute(2, 0, 1), /255
Hyperparametersmanually (SGD, lr 0.01)Optuna se tuned (val set par) — Chapter 22
Resulttest ≈ 0.92train 0.8889, val 0.7068, test 0.7118 (gap 0.1771)

CIFAR-10 mushkil hai: rang, background, alag-alag angles, aur ek class ke andar bahut variety (classes: airplane, automobile, bird, cat, deer, dog, frog, horse, ship, truck). Train–test gap 0.18 = clear overfitting. Lab 13 ke "next improvements" me sabse pehla: data augmentation (phir deeper CNN, LR scheduling, early stopping, zyada Optuna trials, pretrained ResNet).

Augmentation ke common transforms

  • transforms.RandomHorizontalFlip(p=0.5): 50% chance se photo ko left-right mirror. Billi/car ke liye theek; digits/text ke liye nahi (mirror "2" ya "7" label badal deta hai) — Lab 14 (SVHN) ka note: "Do not use horizontal flips; mirrored digits are not label-preserving."
  • transforms.RandomCrop(32, padding=4): pehle har side 4 pixel zero padding (32 → 40×40), phir random jagah se 32×32 kaat lo → photo ±4 pixel tak random khiskti hai (translation).
  • transforms.RandomAffine(degrees=8, translate=(0.08, 0.08), scale=(0.95, 1.05)): chhota rotation, shift, zoom (Lab 14 KMNIST).

PyTorch · train vs test transforms (CIFAR-10)

from torchvision import datasets, transforms

train_transform = transforms.Compose([
    transforms.RandomCrop(32, padding=4),              # random shift (pad 4, phir 32x32 crop)
    transforms.RandomHorizontalFlip(p=0.5),            # random mirror
    transforms.ToTensor(),
    transforms.Normalize((0.5, 0.5, 0.5), (0.5, 0.5, 0.5))   # 3 channels -> 3 values
])
test_transform = transforms.Compose([                  # test par koi randomness NAHI
    transforms.ToTensor(),
    transforms.Normalize((0.5, 0.5, 0.5), (0.5, 0.5, 0.5))
])

train_set = datasets.CIFAR10(root='./data', train=True, download=True, transform=train_transform)
test_set = datasets.CIFAR10(root='./data', train=False, download=True, transform=test_transform)
print(train_set[0][0].shape)        # har baar access par nayi random augmented copy

Output (augmentation pipeline ko ek 32×32 RGB image par chala kar check kiya)

torch.Size([3, 32, 32])
  • On-the-fly: augmentation disk par nayi photos nahi banata; har epoch me har photo ka naya random roop banta hai. Dataset ka size (50,000) wahi rehta hai, lekin model ko har baar thoda alag data dikhta hai.
  • Regularizer ki tarah kaam karta hai → overfitting kam (train–test gap ghatta hai).
  • CNN me jo invariances built-in nahi (flip, chhota rotation, scale), unhe data ke through sikhata hai.
  • Sirf training set par. Validation/test par sirf ToTensor + same Normalize.

Exam Radar

  • CIFAR-10: 32×32×3, 10 classes, 50k train / 10k test. Lab 13 flatten = 4096.
  • Augmentation = label-preserving random transforms, training only, reduces overfitting.
  • RandomCrop(32, padding=4) = random translation up to 4 px; RandomHorizontalFlip(p=0.5) default p = 0.5.
  • Horizontal flip digits/text ke liye galat (label badal sakta hai).

Galti mat karna

  • Test transform me Random... daalna — evaluation random aur unfair ho jaayega.
  • Normalize ke tuples me RGB ke liye 1 hi value dena — 3 chahiye.

Dimaag me aise baitha lo

Augmentation = ek hi billi ki alag-alag selfie. Label wahi, roop naya.

23.23 1×1 convolution — ek chhota preview

Kahani

Juice wale ke paas har glass me 64 alag ras (channels) ki boondein hain. Wo padosi glasses ko dekhta hi nahi; bas har glass ke andar in 64 ras ko alag-alag anupaat me mila kar 32 naye flavours bana deta hai. Glass jitne the utne hi rahe (H × W same), bas flavours (channels) badal gaye. Ye hai 1×1 convolution.

y[o, i, j] = Σc w[o, c] · x[c, i, j] + b[o]
  • x[c, i, j] = input ke channel c me pixel (i, j); o = output channel number
  • w[o, c] = filter o ka channel c wala weight (kernel 1×1, isliye bas ek number per channel)
  • Matlab: har pixel par saare input channels ka weighted sum — ek per-pixel fully connected layer, jo har pixel par shared hai
  • Params = (Cin + 1) × Cout; e.g. 64 → 32: (64 + 1) × 32 = 2,080

Chalo numbers se samjhein

Input: 2 channels, har ek 2×2: A = [1 2; 3 4], B = [5 6; 7 8]. Do 1×1 filters, bias 0: filter 1 = (0.5, 0.5), filter 2 = (1, −1).

  1. Filter 1, pixel (0,0): 0.5×1 + 0.5×5 = 3; poora map = average of A, B = [3 4; 5 6]
  2. Filter 2, pixel (0,0): 1×1 + (−1)×5 = −4; poora map = A − B = [−4 −4; −4 −4]

Jawab: 2×2×2 → 2×2×2; H, W same, channels "mix" ho gaye.

PyTorch · 1×1 conv

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

A = torch.tensor([[[1., 2.], [3., 4.]], [[5., 6.], [7., 8.]]]).unsqueeze(0)   # (1, 2, 2, 2)
w11 = torch.tensor([[[[0.5]], [[0.5]]],      # filter 1: average
                    [[[1.0]], [[-1.0]]]])    # filter 2: difference
print(w11.shape)                             # (C_out=2, C_in=2, 1, 1)
print(F.conv2d(A, w11))

c11 = nn.Conv2d(64, 32, kernel_size=1)       # 64 channels -> 32 channels
print(c11(torch.randn(1, 64, 7, 7)).shape, sum(p.numel() for p in c11.parameters()))

Output

torch.Size([2, 2, 1, 1])
tensor([[[[ 3.,  4.],
          [ 5.,  6.]],

         [[-4., -4.],
          [-4., -4.]]]])
torch.Size([1, 32, 7, 7]) 2080

Kaam kahan aata hai? Mehnge 3×3/5×5 conv se pehle channels kam karne (bottleneck) — L11–12 worksheet: 192 → 128 ka seedha 3×3 = 9 × 192 × 128 = 221,184 weights, jabki pehle 1×1 se 192 → 96 karke phir 3×3: 192 × 96 + 9 × 96 × 128 = 129,024. Ye idea Network-in-Network (2013), Inception (GoogLeNet) aur ResNet bottleneck/projection shortcuts me use hota hai — poori kahani Chapter 24 aur Chapter 25 me.

Exam Radar

  • 1×1 conv: channels mix/change karta hai, H × W same (stride 1), receptive field nahi badhta.
  • Ye saare input channels ko mix karta hai (sirf ek channel ko nahi) — worksheet ka MCQ.
  • Params = (Cin + 1)·Cout; cheap way to reduce channels (dimensionality reduction) + extra ReLU non-linearity.

Dimaag me aise baitha lo

1×1 conv = har glass ke andar ka mixer: padosi nahi dekhta, sirf flavours (channels) badalta hai.

Chapter 24

Classic CNN Architectures — LeNet, AlexNet, VGG, Inception

ImageNet / ILSVRC · top-5 error · LeNet-5 (1998) · AlexNet (2012) · VGG-16/19 (2014) · 1×1 convolution · Inception module · GoogLeNet · Global Average Pooling · depthwise separable conv · comparison

24.1 Kahani ek competition ki: ImageNet aur ILSVRC

Kahani

Socho har saal ek bada "Photo pehchano" cricket tournament hota hai. Har team ko ek machine banani hai. Machine ko ek photo dikhayi jaati hai (kutta, billi, tractor, pizza, jellyfish...) aur machine ko batana hai photo me kya hai. Total 1000 possible jawab hain. Jo team sabse kam galti kare, wahi champion.

2010 aur 2011 me teams purane "haath se banaye features" (hand-crafted features) wale tareeke use karti thi, aur har 4 photo me se lagbhag 1 galat hota tha. Fir 2012 me ek team aayi jisne CNN (wahi convolution wala network jo Chapter 23 me padha) ko bahut bada bana kar GPU pe train kiya. Galti ekdum se 26% se 15% pe aa gayi. Poori duniya hil gayi. Us din se "deep learning ka zamana" shuru hua. Fir har saal nayi team, naya architecture, aur galti aur kam: 2015 tak to machine insaan se bhi kam galti karne lagi.

Ye chapter usi tournament ke champions ki kahani hai: LeNet (dada ji, 1998), AlexNet (2012 ka hero), VGG (2014, "simple par gehra"), GoogLeNet/Inception (2014 champion, "chauda aur smart"). Agla chapter (Chapter 25) 2015 ke champion ResNet ka hai.

Definition

ImageNet: Fei-Fei Li ki team (2009) ka banaya hua ek bahut bada labelled image dataset: lagbhag 14 million images, ~20,000+ categories (WordNet ke naamon par), labelling Amazon Mechanical Turk workers ne ki.

ILSVRC (ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge, 2010–2017): ImageNet ka ek subset jisme 1000 classes, lagbhag 1.2 million (≈1.28M) training images, 50,000 validation aur 100,000 test images hain. Har saal ispe competition hota tha. Jab koi bole "trained on ImageNet", to usually isi 1000-class, 1.2M-image wale subset ki baat hoti hai.

Top-1 error vs Top-5 error (MCQ ka favourite)

Model har photo ke liye 1000 classes ka score (softmax probability) deta hai. Hum scores ko bade se chhote order me lagate hain.

  • Top-1 error: model ka sabse upar wala (pehla) guess galat hai, to error. Strict.
  • Top-5 error: model ke top 5 guesses me sahi label kahin bhi nahi hai, tab hi error. Agar sahi jawab top 5 me kahin bhi hai to "sahi" maana jaata hai. Lenient. Isliye top-5 error hamesha top-1 error se kam ya barabar hota hai.

Top-5 kyun? Kyunki ImageNet me kai photos me ek se zyada cheezein hoti hain (ek photo me "keyboard" bhi hai aur "mouse" bhi) aur kuch classes bahut milti-julti hain ("Siberian husky" vs "Eskimo dog"). Isliye 5 guesses ki chhoot di jaati thi.

Chalo numbers se samjhein

Sawaal: Ek photo ka sahi label hai "Egyptian cat". Model ke scores ke hisaab se top-5 guesses hain: 1. tabby cat (0.41), 2. tiger cat (0.22), 3. Egyptian cat (0.19), 4. lynx (0.06), 5. Persian cat (0.03). 4 aur photos ke top-1 guesses sahi the. Kul 5 photos par top-1 aur top-5 error kya hoga?

  1. Is photo ka pehla guess "tabby cat" hai, sahi label nahi. To top-1 ke hisaab se galat.
  2. Sahi label "Egyptian cat" 3rd number par hai, yaani top-5 ke andar. To top-5 ke hisaab se sahi.
  3. Baaki 4 photos dono hisaab se sahi (jab top-1 sahi hai to top-5 apne aap sahi).
  4. Top-1 error = 1/5 = 20%, Top-5 error = 0/5 = 0%

Jawab: top-1 error 20%, top-5 error 0%. Isliye leaderboards par top-5 number hamesha chhota dikhta hai.

Saal-dar-saal winners (ILSVRC classification, top-5 error)

SaalTeam / ModelTop-5 errorKya khaas tha
2010NEC-UIUC (Lin et al.)≈ 28.2%Hand-crafted features (SIFT, LBP) + linear SVM. No deep learning.
2011XRCE (Perronnin et al.)≈ 25.8%Fisher vectors + SVM. Abhi bhi shallow.
2012AlexNet (SuperVision: Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Hinton)15.3% (runner-up ≈ 26.2%)Pehla bada deep CNN, ReLU, dropout, 2 GPUs. ~11 percentage points ki chhalaang.
2013ZFNet / Clarifai (Zeiler & Fergus)≈ 11.7%AlexNet ko tune kiya: pehli layer 11×11 stride 4 ki jagah 7×7 stride 2; "deconvnet" se filters visualize kiye.
2014GoogLeNet (Inception v1, Szegedy et al.) — winner6.67%Inception module, 1×1 bottleneck, 22 layers, sirf ~5–7M params.
2014VGG (Simonyan & Zisserman) — 2nd7.3% (competition entry; baad me 6.8%)Sirf 3×3 conv, 16–19 layers. Localization task me 1st.
2015ResNet (He, Zhang, Ren, Sun — Microsoft)3.57%Residual (skip) connections, 152 layers. Insaan se behtar.
—Human (Andrej Karpathy ka khud par experiment, 2014)≈ 5.1%Reference line: "human-level".

Ek pattern note karo: har winner pichhle wale se zyada gehra (deeper) tha: AlexNet 8 layers → VGG 16/19 → GoogLeNet 22 → ResNet 152. Hamari slides bhi yahi kehti hain: "there was a general trend for several years for performance on this task to improve as the depth of the networks increased, and this is evidence that depth is important." Par depth badhana muft nahi tha: har architecture ne depth ki kisi na kisi problem ka jugaad nikaala. Wahi jugaad is chapter ka asli syllabus hai.

Exam Radar

  • ILSVRC: 1000 classes, ~1.2M training images, 50k validation, 100k test. Full ImageNet: ~14M images, 20k+ classes.
  • Top-5 error ≤ top-1 error, hamesha. Top-5 = "sahi label top 5 predictions me nahi hai".
  • AlexNet 2012: 15.3% (winning entry). Hamari slides (UDL book) AlexNet ke liye 16.4% top-5, 38.1% top-1 likhti hain — ye 5 CNNs ke average ka number hai bina extra data ke. Dono numbers pehchano: "≈15–16%".
  • VGG: slides me 6.8% top-5, 23.7% top-1 (post-competition best); competition entry 7.3%. GoogLeNet 6.67% ne 2014 jeeta. ResNet 3.57% (2015).
  • Human top-5 error ≈ 5.1% → ResNet (2015) pehla winner jo isse neeche gaya.

Galti mat karna

  • "VGG ne 2014 jeeta" — galat. 2014 classification GoogLeNet ne jeeta; VGG 2nd tha (par localization me 1st).
  • "Top-5 accuracy" aur "top-5 error" ulte hain: accuracy = 100 − error.

Dimaag me aise baitha lo

"28 → 26 → 15 → 12 → 7 → 3.6": SVM, SVM, Alex, ZF, VGG/Google, ResNet. Har kadam = zyada depth + ek naya jugaad.

24.2 Kisi bhi architecture ko padhne ka tareeka (3 formulas + 1 template)

Kahani

Maa jab naya recipe dekhti hain to pehle 3 cheezein dekhti hain: kya-kya dalega (ingredients), kis order me, aur kitni matra me. Architecture bhi ek recipe hai: kaunsi layer, kis order me, kitne filters. Agar tumhe 3 formulas yaad hain, to tum LeNet se ResNet tak har table khud bhar sakte ho — exam me bhi yahi poocha jaata hai.

Output size: O = ⌊ W − K + 2PS ⌋ + 1
Conv params = (K · K · Cin + 1) · Cout   |   FC params = (Nin + 1) · Nout
  • W = input ki height/width, K = kernel (filter) size, P = padding, S = stride, ⌊ ⌋ = neeche round (floor).
  • Cin = input channels (filter ki depth hamesha input ki depth ke barabar), Cout = filters ki ginti = output channels.
  • "+1" = har filter / har neuron ka ek bias.
  • Pooling, ReLU, Flatten, Dropout, Softmax, (original) LRN: 0 parameters. Pooling channels nahi badalta.

Ye teeno Chapter 23 me derive ho chuke hain; yahan sirf use karenge. Do aur zaroori baatein:

  • Naam me jo number hai (LeNet-5, VGG-16, ResNet-50) wo usually sirf "weight wali" layers ginta hai — conv + FC. Pooling/ReLU/BN nahi gine jaate. (LeNet-5 ka "5" thoda alag hai — neeche dekhenge.)
  • Activations vs parameters: activation = ek image ke liye bana output (feature map), har image ke saath badalta hai. Parameter = seekha hua weight, sab images ke liye same. Batch size double karo to activations double, parameters same. (Teacher ka L11 quiz: "Double the batch size — trainable parameter count? → It stays the same.")

Classic CNN template

Saare classic CNNs ek hi dhaanche par bane hain: [CONV → ReLU/tanh → (CONV …) → POOL] × n → FLATTEN → FC → FC → softmax. Jaise jaise aage badhte hain: spatial size (H×W) chhota hota jaata hai, channels (depth) badhte jaate hain. Matlab network "kahan hai" wali detail chhodta jaata hai aur "kya hai" wali samajh (rich features) badhata jaata hai. Teacher ke L11 page ke "Three ideas" yahi the: (1) spatial size aur channel count alag kaam karte hain; (2) activations aur parameters alag cheezein hain; (3) fully connected layers parameter budget pe kabza kar leti hain.

24.3 LeNet-5 (1998) — CNN ke dada ji, bank ke cheque padhne wale

Kahani

1990s ka America. Banks me roz laakhon cheques aate the, aur har cheque pe haath se likha amount kisi insaan ko padh kar computer me type karna padta tha. Thakaau, mehenga, galti wala kaam. AT&T Bell Labs me Yann LeCun aur saathiyon (Léon Bottou, Yoshua Bengio, Patrick Haffner) ne ek chhota sa network banaya jo haath se likhe digits padh leta tha. Paper: "Gradient-Based Learning Applied to Document Recognition", Proceedings of the IEEE, 1998. Paper ke mutabik ye system US ke kai banks me har mahine laakhon cheques padh raha tha.

Iska naam tha LeNet-5. Aaj ke standard se ye bachcha hai (sirf ~60 hazaar parameters), par isme wo saari cheezein pehli baar ek saath dikhi jo aaj har CNN me hain: local receptive field, weight sharing, pooling (subsampling), feature hierarchy, aur end-to-end backprop training.

Dataset: MNIST

MNIST = haath se likhe digits 0–9 ka dataset: 60,000 training + 10,000 test images, har image 28×28 grayscale (1 channel). LeNet-5 ka input 32×32 tha: digit ko 32×32 frame ke beech me rakha jaata tha (2 pixel ka border), taaki stroke ke end-points aur corners bhi filters ke receptive field ke beech me aa sakein. Isliye MNIST ke saath modern code me pehli conv me padding=2 lagate hain (28 + 2·2 = 32 jaisa effect).

Architecture: C1 → S2 → C3 → S4 → C5 → F6 → Output

Original paper me naam aise the: C = convolution layer, S = subsampling (pooling) layer, F = fully connected. Pattern yaad rakho: conv → pool → conv → pool → conv(fc) → fc → output.

Layer-by-layer table (original LeNet-5, 1998)

LayerKya karta haiOutput shapeParameters (calculation)
Inputgrayscale digit32×32×10
C16 filters, 5×5, stride 1, no padding28×28×6  (32−5+1 = 28)(5·5·1 + 1)·6 = 156
S22×2 subsampling, stride 2 (har map ka 1 trainable coefficient + 1 bias)14×14×62·6 = 12 (modern avg/max pool me 0)
C316 filters, 5×5, partial connections to S2 maps10×10×16  (14−5+1 = 10)1,516 original  |  (5·5·6 + 1)·16 = 2,416 agar full connected
S42×2 subsampling, stride 25×5×162·16 = 32 (modern me 0)
C5120 filters, 5×5×16 (filter = poora input!)1×1×120  (5−5+1 = 1)(5·5·16 + 1)·120 = 48,120
F6fully connected, 84 neurons, tanh84(120 + 1)·84 = 10,164
Output10 units (original: Euclidean RBF; modern: Linear + softmax)10modern: (84 + 1)·10 = 850 (original RBF ke 84·10 = 840 fixed values)

Chalo numbers se samjhein — total ≈ 60k kaise?

  1. C3 ke partial connections (paper ka table): pehle 6 maps, S2 ke 3 lagatar maps se jude; agle 6 maps 4 lagatar maps se; agle 3 maps 4 non-lagatar maps se; aakhri 1 map saare 6 se. Ek map jo k input maps dekhta hai uske params = k·25 + 1.
    6·(3·25+1) + 6·(4·25+1) + 3·(4·25+1) + 1·(6·25+1)
    = 6·76 + 6·101 + 3·101 + 151
    = 456 + 606 + 303 + 151 = 1,516
  2. Ab original trainable params jodo: 156 + 12 + 1,516 + 32 + 48,120 + 10,164 = 60,000. Paper bhi exactly yahi kehta hai: "340,908 connections, but only 60,000 trainable free parameters". (Connections zyada kyunki ek hi weight bahut jagah reuse hota hai — weight sharing.)
  3. Modern version (C3 full, pooling me 0 params, Linear(84,10)): 156 + 0 + 2,416 + 0 + 48,120 + 10,164 + 850 = 61,706.
  4. Teacher ke L11 page ka split: conv (C1 + C3) = 156 + 2,416 = 2,572; baaki "fully connected" (400→120, 120→84, 84→10) = 48,120 + 10,164 + 850 = 59,134. 59,134 / 61,706 = 95.8% params FC part me!

Jawab: original ≈ 60,000 params; modern PyTorch/Keras version = 61,706 params, jisme ~95.8% fully connected hisse me.

Original LeNet ki khaas baatein (jo aaj badal gayi)

  • Activation: scaled tanh, f(a) = 1.7159 · tanh(2a/3) (sigmoid jaisa S-shape). ReLU tab popular nahi tha.
  • Pooling: "subsampling" = 2×2 ka average × trainable coefficient + bias, fir sigmoid. Aaj ka modern version: average ya max pooling, 0 params.
  • C3 partial connectivity: do wajah — (1) parameters kam, (2) symmetry todna: alag maps ko alag input combinations milein to wo alag features seekhein.
  • C5 technically convolution hai, par 5×5 input pe 5×5 filter → output 1×1, isliye ye practically ek fully connected layer ki tarah kaam karta hai. Modern code me ise Flatten + nn.Linear(400, 120) likhte hain — dono ke params same: 48,120.
  • F6 = 84 kyun? Output RBF units har character ko 7×12 = 84 pixel ke bitmap code se compare karte the. Isliye 84.
  • Output: 10 Euclidean RBF units (input ka distance ek fixed prototype se). Aaj: Linear + softmax + cross-entropy.
  • Result: MNIST test error 0.95% (distorted extra training data ke saath 0.8%).
  • Naam "LeNet-5": LeNet series ka 5th model. "5 layers" matlab nahi — paper input ke baad 7 layers (C1, S2, C3, S4, C5, F6, Output) ginta hai. (Modern ginti me weight wali layers C1, C3, C5, F6, Output = 5 bhi ban jaati hain — isliye kai jagah "5 learnable layers" likha milta hai.)

Receptive field kaise badhta hai (LeNet study notes ka table)

StageInputC1S2C3S4C5
Original image me receptive field1×15×56×614×1416×1632×32 (poori image)

C1 ka ek neuron sirf ek chhota stroke dekhta hai; C5 ka ek neuron poora digit "dekh" sakta hai. Yahi feature hierarchy hai: edges/strokes → stroke combinations → poora digit.

RGB input ho to kya badlega?

Agar input 32×32×3 ho, to C1 ka har filter 5×5×3 hoga (filter depth = input depth). (5·5·3 + 1)·6 = 76·6 = 456 params. Output phir bhi 28×28×6 (6 filters → 6 maps; ek filter RGB teeno ko jod kar ek hi map banata hai). C1 ke baad ki layers bilkul same.

PyTorch: modern LeNet-5 for 28×28 MNIST

Naya API yahan: nn.AvgPool2d(kernel_size, stride) — window ka average leta hai (max ki jagah). Default stride = kernel_size. Params: 0. nn.Tanh() — tanh activation as a layer.

PyTorch · LeNet-5 (teacher notebook ka Keras model, PyTorch me)

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class LeNet5(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, num_classes=10):
        super().__init__()
        self.features = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(1, 6, kernel_size=5, padding=2),   # C1: (N,1,28,28) -> (N,6,28,28)  padding=2 se 28 hi raha
            nn.Tanh(),                                   # original jaisa tanh (modern: nn.ReLU())
            nn.AvgPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2),       # S2: -> (N,6,14,14)
            nn.Conv2d(6, 16, kernel_size=5),             # C3: -> (N,16,10,10)   14-5+1 = 10
            nn.Tanh(),
            nn.AvgPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2),       # S4: -> (N,16,5,5)
        )
        self.classifier = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Flatten(),                                # 16*5*5 = 400 numbers ki line
            nn.Linear(16 * 5 * 5, 120),                  # C5 ka kaam: 400 -> 120
            nn.Tanh(),
            nn.Linear(120, 84),                          # F6: 120 -> 84
            nn.Tanh(),
            nn.Linear(84, num_classes),                  # output logits (softmax CrossEntropyLoss ke andar)
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.features(x)
        return self.classifier(x)

model = LeNet5()
x = torch.randn(1, 1, 28, 28)            # ek fake MNIST image: (batch, channel, H, W)
for layer in list(model.features) + list(model.classifier):
    x = layer(x)                         # layer by layer chalao aur shape dekho
    print(f"{layer.__class__.__name__:10s} -> {tuple(x.shape)}")

total = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())   # numel() = tensor me kitne numbers
print("Total params:", total)

Output

Conv2d     -> (1, 6, 28, 28)
Tanh       -> (1, 6, 28, 28)
AvgPool2d  -> (1, 6, 14, 14)
Conv2d     -> (1, 16, 10, 10)
Tanh       -> (1, 16, 10, 10)
AvgPool2d  -> (1, 16, 5, 5)
Flatten    -> (1, 400)
Linear     -> (1, 120)
Tanh       -> (1, 120)
Linear     -> (1, 84)
Tanh       -> (1, 84)
Linear     -> (1, 10)
Total params: 61706

Parameter counting ka one-liner yaad kar lo: sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()). Sirf trainable chahiye to: sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters() if p.requires_grad). model.parameters() saare weight aur bias tensors deta hai; p.numel() us tensor ke elements ginta hai (jaise C1 weight ka shape (6,1,5,5) → 150).

Training bilkul wahi standard loop hai (Chapter 13): criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss(), optimizer = optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3), phir har batch par zero_grad → forward → loss → backward → step. Teacher ke Keras notebook me (tanh + average pooling, Adam, batch 128) sirf 5 epochs me MNIST test accuracy 98.35% aayi thi.

Flatten se pehle 16·5·5 = 400 khud calculate karna — exam me Linear ka in_features yahi poochte hain.

Exam Radar

  • LeNet-5: LeCun, Bottou, Bengio, Haffner, 1998; task: handwritten digits / bank cheque reading; dataset MNIST.
  • Input 32×32×1; C1 6@5×5 → 28×28×6; S2 → 14×14×6; C3 16@5×5 → 10×10×16; S4 → 5×5×16; C5 120 → 1×1×120; F6 84; output 10.
  • Params: C1 156, C3 1,516 (original) / 2,416 (full), C5 48,120, F6 10,164, output 850 (modern). Total ≈ 60k (modern 61,706).
  • Activation: tanh/sigmoid (scaled tanh 1.7159·tanh(2a/3)); pooling: average (subsampling). No ReLU, no dropout, no max-pool in original.
  • Pattern: conv-pool-conv-pool-fc-fc-output. Spatial 32→28→14→10→5→1, depth 1→6→16→120.
  • ~95.8% params FC hisse me (modern version) — "FC layers dominate the parameter budget".

Galti mat karna

  • C3 ke params pooche to dekho source "original" bol raha hai (1,516) ya "modern Conv2d" (2,416). Dono sahi ho sakte hain — context padho.
  • RGB input pe C1 filter 5×5 nahi, 5×5×3 hai; ek filter = ek feature map (teen nahi).
  • 28×28 MNIST pe padding=0 lagaya to C1 ke baad 24×24, aakhir me 4×4×16 = 256 aayega, aur nn.Linear(400,120) shape error dega. Ya padding=2 lagao ya Linear(256,120).

Dimaag me aise baitha lo

"6-16-120-84-10" — LeNet ka phone number. Aur "156 · 2416 · 48120 · 10164 · 850" = 61,706.

24.4 AlexNet (2012) — jisne deep learning ka zamana shuru kiya

Kahani

Toronto University me Geoffrey Hinton ke student Alex Krizhevsky aur Ilya Sutskever ne socha: "LeNet wala idea hi lo, par isko bahut bada karo, aur 1.2 million rangeen photos pe train karo." Problem: itna bada network us zamane ke CPU pe mahino chalta. Jugaad: gaming wale graphics cards! Unhone network ko do NVIDIA GTX 580 GPUs (3 GB each) pe baant diya aur ~5–6 din train kiya.

Result: ILSVRC 2012 me top-5 error 15.3%, jabki doosre number ki team (purane hand-crafted features) 26.2% pe thi. Socho cricket me ek team 350 banaye aur doosri 180 — sab log samajh gaye ki khel badal gaya hai. Paper: "ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks", Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Hinton, NIPS 2012.

Slides (UDL book) ke shabdon me: "AlexNet ... consists of eight hidden layers with ReLU activation functions, of which the first five are convolutional and the rest fully connected." Matlab 8 learned layers = 5 conv + 3 FC. Paper ke hisaab se ~60 million parameters aur ~650,000 neurons.

Layer table (single-GPU "standard" version, input 227×227×3)

Paper me input 224×224 likha hai, par us par formula integer nahi deta: (224 − 11)/4 + 1 = 54.25. Isliye textbooks/teacher ka notebook 227×227×3 lete hain: (227 − 11)/4 + 1 = 216/4 + 1 = 55 ✓. (torchvision 224 + padding 2 leta hai: ⌊(224 − 11 + 4)/4⌋ + 1 = 55.)

LayerSettingsOutput shapeSize calculationParameters
InputRGB227×227×3—0
Conv196 filters 11×11, stride 4, pad 0, ReLU (+LRN)55×55×96(227−11)/4+1 = 55(11·11·3+1)·96 = 34,944
MaxPool13×3, stride 2 (overlapping)27×27×96⌊(55−3)/2⌋+1 = 270
Conv2256 filters 5×5, pad 2, ReLU (+LRN)27×27×256(27−5+4)/1+1 = 27(5·5·96+1)·256 = 614,656
MaxPool23×3, stride 213×13×256⌊(27−3)/2⌋+1 = 130
Conv3384 filters 3×3, pad 1, ReLU13×13×384(13−3+2)+1 = 13(3·3·256+1)·384 = 885,120
Conv4384 filters 3×3, pad 1, ReLU13×13×38413(3·3·384+1)·384 = 1,327,488
Conv5256 filters 3×3, pad 1, ReLU13×13×25613(3·3·384+1)·256 = 884,992
MaxPool33×3, stride 26×6×256⌊(13−3)/2⌋+1 = 60
Flatten—9,2166·6·2560
FC64096, ReLU, dropout 0.54096—(9216+1)·4096 = 37,752,832
FC74096, ReLU, dropout 0.54096—(4096+1)·4096 = 16,781,312
FC81000, softmax1000—(4096+1)·1000 = 4,097,000
Total (teacher ke L11 page ka number bhi yahi)62,378,344 ≈ 62.4M

Chalo numbers se samjhein — paisa kahan gaya?

  1. Saare conv layers: 34,944 + 614,656 + 885,120 + 1,327,488 + 884,992 = 3,747,200 (≈ 3.7M).
  2. Saare FC layers: 37,752,832 + 16,781,312 + 4,097,000 = 58,631,144 (≈ 58.6M).
  3. FC ka hissa: 58,631,144 / 62,378,344 = 94.0%. Akela FC6: 37,752,832 / 62,378,344 = 60.5%.
  4. Original paper me Conv2, Conv4, Conv5 do GPUs me bate the (har filter sirf apne GPU ke aadhe channels dekhta tha — PyTorch me groups=2). Tab: Conv2 = (5·5·48+1)·256 = 307,456; Conv4 = (3·3·192+1)·384 = 663,936; Conv5 = (3·3·192+1)·256 = 442,624 → total 60,965,224 ≈ 61M. Isliye paper "60 million" bolta hai.

Jawab: ~62.4M (single-tower) / ~61M (original 2-GPU). 94% params FC me; sabse bhaari layer FC6 (~37.7M). Teacher ke L11 quiz ka jawab: "Which layer contributes the most trainable parameters? → FC 1 (yaani FC6)".

AlexNet ke 7 innovations (MCQ yahin se aate hain)

#IdeaKya kiya / kyun
1ReLU activationtanh/sigmoid ki jagah max(0, x). Positive side pe saturate nahi hota → gradient zinda. Paper: 4-layer CNN ne CIFAR-10 pe 25% training error tak ~6× tezi se pahuncha tanh ke mukable. (Chapter 9)
2Dropout 0.5FC6 aur FC7 me. 60M params ke saath overfitting ka bada dar tha. Dropout ne overfitting roka par convergence ke liye ~2× iterations lage. (Chapter 20)
3Data augmentation(a) 256×256 image se random 224×224 crops + horizontal flips (data ~2048× "bada"); (b) PCA colour augmentation: RGB intensities me principal components ke along random badlav (lighting change jaisa) — top-1 error 1% se zyada kam. Test time pe 10 patches (4 corners + centre, aur unke flips) ka average.
4LRN (Local Response Normalization)Conv1, Conv2 ke ReLU ke baad. Ek position par padosi channels ke beech "lateral inhibition": bada response baakiyon ko daba deta hai. Top-1/top-5 me ~1.4%/1.2% sudhaar. 0 params. Baad me (VGG ne dikhaya ki khaas fayda nahi; aur BatchNorm ne replace kar diya) chhod diya gaya.
5Overlapping max poolingWindow 3×3, stride 2 (window > stride, to windows overlap). Non-overlapping 2×2/2 ke mukable top-1/top-5 ~0.4%/0.3% behtar, overfitting thoda kam.
6Multi-GPU trainingNetwork 2 × GTX 580 (3GB) pe split; GPUs sirf kuch layers pe baat karte the. ~5–6 din training.
7Training recipeSGD + momentum 0.9, weight decay 0.0005, batch size 128, lr = 0.01, validation error ruk jaye to lr ÷ 10 (3 baar hua), ~90 epochs. Weights init N(0, 0.01²).

LeNet-5 (1998)

32×32×1 digits · 2 conv + 3 FC · tanh/sigmoid · average pooling · ~60k params · CPU · no dropout · MNIST (10 classes)

AlexNet (2012)

227×227×3 photos · 5 conv + 3 FC · ReLU · overlapping max pooling · ~60M params (1000× zyada) · 2 GPUs · dropout + augmentation · ImageNet (1000 classes)

Teacher ke notebook ki line yaad rakho: "LeNet: CNN works → AlexNet: CNN scales → VGG: CNN goes deeper."

PyTorch: compact AlexNet (ImageNet shape, single tower)

Naye arguments: nn.ReLU(inplace=True) — output alag tensor me banane ki jagah input ko hi overwrite karta hai (memory bachti hai, result same). nn.Dropout(p=0.5) — training me 50% neurons random band (Chapter 20); model.eval() me automatically band.

PyTorch · AlexNet (227×227 input)

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class AlexNet(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, num_classes=1000):
        super().__init__()
        self.features = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(3, 96, kernel_size=11, stride=4),          # (N,3,227,227) -> (N,96,55,55)
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
            nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=3, stride=2),               # -> (N,96,27,27)  overlapping pool
            nn.Conv2d(96, 256, kernel_size=5, padding=2),        # -> (N,256,27,27)
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
            nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=3, stride=2),               # -> (N,256,13,13)
            nn.Conv2d(256, 384, kernel_size=3, padding=1),       # -> (N,384,13,13)
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
            nn.Conv2d(384, 384, kernel_size=3, padding=1),       # -> (N,384,13,13)
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
            nn.Conv2d(384, 256, kernel_size=3, padding=1),       # -> (N,256,13,13)
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
            nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=3, stride=2),               # -> (N,256,6,6)
        )
        self.classifier = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Flatten(),                                        # -> (N,9216)
            nn.Dropout(p=0.5),
            nn.Linear(256 * 6 * 6, 4096),                        # FC6 (sabse bhaari)
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
            nn.Dropout(p=0.5),
            nn.Linear(4096, 4096),                               # FC7
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
            nn.Linear(4096, num_classes),                        # FC8 -> logits (softmax loss ke andar)
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.classifier(self.features(x))

model = AlexNet()
x = torch.randn(2, 3, 227, 227)                     # dummy batch of 2 images
print("features out:", tuple(model.features(x).shape))
print("logits      :", tuple(model(x).shape))
total = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())
fc6 = model.classifier[2].weight.numel() + model.classifier[2].bias.numel()
print(f"Total params: {total:,}")
print(f"FC6 params  : {fc6:,}  ({100*fc6/total:.1f}% of total)")

Output

features out: (2, 256, 6, 6)
logits      : (2, 1000)
Total params: 62,378,344
FC6 params  : 37,752,832  (60.5% of total)
  • torchvision.models.alexnet() thoda alag "one weird trick" version hai (channels 64-192-384-256-256, beech me AdaptiveAvgPool2d((6,6))): 61,100,840 params. Number dekh ke ghabrana mat.
  • Lab 15 (CIFAR-10, 32×32): 11×11 stride 4 lagaya to 32×32 image pehli layer me hi ~6×6 ho jaati, isliye lab ne saare kernels 3×3 (padding='same') aur 2×2 pooling rakhe: channels 64→192→384→256→256, flatten 256·4·4 = 4096, fir Dropout + Linear(4096,4096) + ReLU + Dropout + Linear(4096,4096) + ReLU + Linear(4096,10) (do 4096-wali FC layers, AlexNet jaisa). Params ≈ 35.9M, jisme ~94% FC me. Result (10 epochs): train 88.87%, test 77.34% — baseline CNN (train 97.97%, test 72.23%) se overfitting kam.

Exam Radar

  • Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Hinton — 2012, ILSVRC 2012 winner, top-5 15.3% (slides: 16.4% top-5, 38.1% top-1).
  • 8 layers = 5 conv + 3 FC. Filters 96→256→384→384→256; FC 4096→4096→1000.
  • Conv1: 96 @ 11×11, stride 4 → 55×55×96. Pools: 3×3 stride 2 (overlapping). Last conv output 6×6×256 = 9216.
  • Params ≈ 60–62M; FC6 ≈ 37.7M (largest); ~94% FC.
  • Innovations: ReLU (≈6× faster than tanh), dropout 0.5, data augmentation (crops, flips, PCA colour), LRN, overlapping pooling, 2 GPUs (GTX 580).
  • Training: SGD momentum 0.9, weight decay 5e-4, lr 0.01 ÷10 on plateau, batch 128.

Galti mat karna

  • "AlexNet ne pehli baar CNN banaya" — nahi! CNN (LeNet) 1998 se tha. AlexNet ne dikhaya ki CNN bade data + GPU + ReLU + dropout ke saath scale hota hai.
  • 224 vs 227: formula 224 pe integer nahi deta; 227 lo (ya 224 + padding 2).
  • AlexNet me BatchNorm nahi tha (BN 2015 me aaya). Uski normalization = LRN.

Dimaag me aise baitha lo

"11-4-96" (pehli layer), "R-D-A-L-O-G": ReLU, Dropout, Augmentation, LRN, Overlapping pool, GPUs.

24.5 VGG (2014) — "ek hi chhoti eent, bahut oonchi deewar"

Kahani

AlexNet ek "jugaadu" building jaisa tha: kahin 11×11 ki khidki, kahin 5×5, kahin 3×3; kahin LRN, kahin nahi. Oxford University ke Visual Geometry Group (VGG) ke Karen Simonyan aur Andrew Zisserman ne socha: "Agar hum sirf ek hi size ki chhoti eent (3×3 conv) use karein, aur deewar ko bas oonchi (deeper) karte jaayein, to kya hoga?" Jaise Lego me ek hi tarah ke chhote bricks se poora mahal ban jaata hai.

Result: 16 aur 19 layers ke networks — VGG-16 aur VGG-19 — jo AlexNet se kaafi behtar the. Paper: "Very Deep Convolutional Networks for Large-Scale Image Recognition" (arXiv 2014, ICLR 2015). ILSVRC 2014 me classification me 2nd (7.3%, baad me 6.8%) aur localization me 1st. Iski simplicity ki wajah se aaj bhi ye teaching aur transfer learning ka favourite hai.

VGG ke design rules (poora architecture inhi 4 lines me)

1. Har convolution: 3×3 kernel, stride 1, padding 1 → spatial size same rehta hai: (224 − 3 + 2·1)/1 + 1 = 224.
2. Har block ke end me 2×2 max-pool, stride 2 → size aadha.
3. Har pool ke baad channels double: 64 → 128 → 256 → 512 → 512 (512 pe cap).
4. Aakhir me 3 FC: 4096 → 4096 → 1000 (+ softmax). Har conv/FC ke baad ReLU. FC1, FC2 me dropout 0.5.

Paper ne 5 configurations try ki (A se E): A = 11 layers (VGG-11), B = 13, C = 16 (kuch 1×1 conv ke saath), D = 16 layers (VGG-16), E = 19 layers (VGG-19). Params: A ≈ 133M, D ≈ 138M, E ≈ 144M. Depth badhane se error ghatta gaya (D aur E sabse achhe) — "depth matters" ka saboot.

VGG-16 full table (config D, input 224×224×3)

Config list jo code me bhi likhenge: [64, 64, M, 128, 128, M, 256, 256, 256, M, 512, 512, 512, M, 512, 512, 512, M] (M = maxpool). Blocks me conv ki ginti: 2, 2, 3, 3, 3 = 13 conv. Plus 3 FC = 16 weight layers. (5 max-pools aur ReLUs "16" me nahi gine jaate.)

Chalo numbers se samjhein

  1. Conv1_2 ke params Conv1_1 se zyada kyun, jabki dono 64 channels banate hain? Kyunki Conv1_2 ka input 64 channels hai (Conv1_1 ka sirf 3): (3·3·64 + 1)·64 = 577·64 = 36,928 vs (3·3·3 + 1)·64 = 28·64 = 1,792. (Teacher ka L11 quiz bhi yahi tha: "It receives 64 input channels instead of 3".)
  2. Conv4_2: ek filter = 3·3·512 = 4,608 weights, +1 bias = 4,609; 512 filters → 4,609 × 512 = 2,359,808.
  3. FC1: (25,088 + 1) × 4,096 = 102,764,544. Ye akela poore network ka 102,764,544 / 138,357,544 = 74.3% hai!
  4. Teeno FC: 123,642,856 / 138,357,544 = 89.4%. Conv backbone sirf 14.7M (10.6%).

Jawab: VGG-16 = 138,357,544 params; ~124M (89.4%) teen FC layers me, FC1 akela ~102.8M. VGG-19 (3 extra conv 512-channel layers) = 143,667,240 ≈ 144M.

Sabse important sawaal: sirf 3×3 hi kyun?

Socho tum chhat pe khade ho aur neeche ka ilaaka dekhna hai. Ek tareeka: ek badi 7×7 khidki. Doosra: 3 chhoti 3×3 khidkiyan ek ke upar ek. Teen fayde:

  1. Same receptive field: pehli 3×3 layer ka ek neuron input ka 3×3 dekhta hai. Doosri 3×3 layer ka neuron pehli layer ke 3×3 neurons dekhta hai, jinme har ek 3×3 dekhta hai aur wo ek-ek pixel khiske hue hain → input ka (3 + 2) = 5×5. Teesri layer → (5 + 2) = 7×7. General: n stacked 3×3 (stride 1) ka receptive field = 2n + 1.
  2. Kam parameters (maan lo input aur output dono me C channels, bias ignore):
    Ek 5×5 conv: 5·5·C·C = 25C² vs do 3×3: 2·(3·3·C·C) = 18C² → 28% kam
    Ek 7×7 conv: 7·7·C·C = 49C² vs teen 3×3: 3·(9C²) = 27C² → 45% kam
    C = 64 pe: 25C² = 102,400 vs 18C² = 73,728 · 49C² = 200,704 vs 27C² = 110,592
  3. Zyada non-linearity: teen layers = teen ReLU, ek 7×7 = sirf ek ReLU. Zyada ReLU → decision function zyada "discriminative" (complex patterns pakad sakta hai). Paper isko ek tarah ka regularization bhi bolta hai: 7×7 filter ko majboor kiya ki wo 3×3 ke combination me toote.

Receptive field VGG-16 me kitna bada hota hai

VGG study notes ka table (theoretical receptive field, original image pixels me): Conv1_1: 3 · Conv1_2: 5 · Pool1: 6 · Conv2_2: 14 · Pool2: 16 · Conv3_3: 40 · Pool3: 44 · Conv4_3: 92 · Pool4: 100 · Conv5_3: 196 · Pool5: 212. Matlab aakhri conv ka ek neuron 224×224 image ka lagbhag poora hissa "dekh" sakta hai — chhote filters, bada nazaara.

VGG ki kamzoriyan (drawbacks)

  • Bahut bhaari: ~138M params; pretrained weights file ≈ 528 MB (teacher notebook). Mobile pe chalana mushkil.
  • Slow: ek image ke liye ~15 billion multiply-adds (AlexNet se kai guna). 224×224 resolution pe 64 channels wali pehli layers sabse mehngi (compute), FC1 sabse mehngi (params).
  • Memory: forward pass me ek image ke ~15.2 million activation values (float32 me ≈ 61 MB), backward ke liye aur zyada.
  • FC layers ka bojh: 89% params sirf classifier me — aage ke models (GoogLeNet, ResNet) ne isko global average pooling se hata diya.
  • Skip connections nahi: aur gehra karna (VGG-30, VGG-50) mushkil — training hi nahi hoti thi. Original VGG me BatchNorm bhi nahi tha; paper ne deep configs ko shallow config A ke trained weights se initialize kiya tha taaki training shuru ho sake. Ye "depth ki deewar" ResNet ne todi (Chapter 25).

Training recipe (AlexNet jaisa hi): mini-batch SGD, batch 256, momentum 0.9, weight decay 5·10−4, dropout 0.5 (FC1, FC2), lr 0.01 ÷ 10 jab validation accuracy ruk jaaye (3 baar), ~74 epochs, 4 GPUs pe 2–3 hafte. Input: 224×224 RGB jisme training set ka mean RGB subtract kiya.

PyTorch: config list se VGG banana (make_layers)

Ye trick exam me favourite hai: list ke har number pe conv+ReLU, har 'M' pe maxpool. nn.Sequential(*layers) me * list ko unpack karke alag-alag arguments bana deta hai.

PyTorch · VGG-16 from a config list

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

cfg_vgg16 = [64, 64, 'M', 128, 128, 'M', 256, 256, 256, 'M',
             512, 512, 512, 'M', 512, 512, 512, 'M']

def make_layers(cfg, in_channels=3):
    layers = []
    for v in cfg:
        if v == 'M':
            layers.append(nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2))   # size aadha
        else:
            layers.append(nn.Conv2d(in_channels, v, kernel_size=3, padding=1))  # size same
            layers.append(nn.ReLU(inplace=True))
            in_channels = v                                         # agle conv ka C_in = ye v
    return nn.Sequential(*layers)

class VGG16(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, num_classes=1000):
        super().__init__()
        self.features = make_layers(cfg_vgg16)          # 13 conv layers
        self.classifier = nn.Sequential(                 # 3 FC layers
            nn.Flatten(),
            nn.Linear(512 * 7 * 7, 4096), nn.ReLU(inplace=True), nn.Dropout(0.5),
            nn.Linear(4096, 4096),        nn.ReLU(inplace=True), nn.Dropout(0.5),
            nn.Linear(4096, num_classes),
        )
    def forward(self, x):
        return self.classifier(self.features(x))

model = VGG16()
x = torch.randn(1, 3, 224, 224)
print("after features:", tuple(model.features(x).shape))
print("logits        :", tuple(model(x).shape))
n_conv = sum(isinstance(m, nn.Conv2d) for m in model.modules())   # modules() = saari sub-layers
n_fc = sum(isinstance(m, nn.Linear) for m in model.modules())
conv_p = sum(p.numel() for p in model.features.parameters())
total = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())
print("conv layers:", n_conv, "| fc layers:", n_fc)
print(f"conv params: {conv_p:,} | total: {total:,}")

Output

after features: (1, 512, 7, 7)
logits        : (1, 1000)
conv layers: 13 | fc layers: 3
conv params: 14,714,688 | total: 138,357,544

VGG-19 banana ho to sirf list badlo: [64,64,'M',128,128,'M',256,256,256,256,'M',512,512,512,512,'M',512,512,512,512,'M'] (blocks 2,2,4,4,4 = 16 conv + 3 FC = 19). Wahi function, naya network — yahi VGG ki khoobsurti hai.

torchvision ka ready-made VGG + transfer learning

torchvision.models.vgg16(weights=...): weights=None → random init; weights=models.VGG16_Weights.IMAGENET1K_V1 → ImageNet pe trained weights download. torchvision ke VGG me features (13 conv), avgpool (AdaptiveAvgPool2d((7,7))) aur classifier (index 0 se 6; aakhri Linear classifier[6]) hote hain. Transfer learning: pretrained conv backbone ko freeze karo (requires_grad = False), sirf naya head train karo.

PyTorch · VGG-16 transfer learning (5 classes)

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torchvision import models

vgg = models.vgg16(weights=None)   # asli kaam me: weights=models.VGG16_Weights.IMAGENET1K_V1 (~528 MB)
for p in vgg.features.parameters():
    p.requires_grad = False        # conv backbone freeze: ye weights update nahi honge
vgg.classifier[6] = nn.Linear(4096, 5)   # 1000 classes ki jagah humari 5 classes

trainable = sum(p.numel() for p in vgg.parameters() if p.requires_grad)
frozen = sum(p.numel() for p in vgg.parameters() if not p.requires_grad)
print(f"trainable: {trainable:,} | frozen: {frozen:,}")
print(vgg(torch.randn(1, 3, 224, 224)).shape)

Output

trainable: 119,566,341 | frozen: 14,714,688
torch.Size([1, 5])

Optimizer ko sirf trainable params do: optim.Adam(filter(lambda p: p.requires_grad, vgg.parameters()), lr=1e-4) (ya seedha vgg.classifier.parameters()). Baad me chaho to deeper conv blocks unfreeze karke chhote lr se fine-tune karo.

Lab 15 ka VGG-style (CIFAR-10): sirf 3×3 convs (64→128→256→256→512→512→512→512), har conv ke baad BatchNorm2d (original VGG me BN nahi tha; BN 2015 me aaya — torchvision me alag model vgg16_bn hai), aur chhota head (sirf Linear(512, 10)). Params ≈ 9.2M, FC params sirf ~5k. Result: train 96.68%, test 81.76% — lab ka best test accuracy.

Exam Radar

  • Simonyan & Zisserman, Oxford (Visual Geometry Group), 2014. ILSVRC 2014: classification 2nd (7.3%), localization 1st. Slides: 6.8% top-5, 23.7% top-1.
  • Sirf 3×3 conv (stride 1, pad 1) + 2×2 max-pool (stride 2); channels 64→128→256→512→512; spatial 224→112→56→28→14→7.
  • VGG-16 = 13 conv + 3 FC; blocks 2-2-3-3-3; VGG-19 = 16 conv + 3 FC; blocks 2-2-4-4-4.
  • Params: VGG-16 ≈ 138M (138,357,544), VGG-19 ≈ 144M. FC ≈ 124M (89%), FC1 ≈ 102.8M (74%). Flatten = 7·7·512 = 25,088.
  • Two 3×3 = 5×5 RF (18C² vs 25C²); three 3×3 = 7×7 RF (27C² vs 49C²) + more ReLUs.
  • Drawbacks: memory, slow, huge FC head, no skip connections. Use today: transfer learning / feature extractor.

Galti mat karna

  • VGG me conv layers size nahi ghatate (padding 1, stride 1); size sirf pooling se ghatta hai. (L11 quiz: "Where does the image become spatially smaller? → At the max-pooling layer".)
  • "VGG-16 me 16 conv layers" — galat; 13 conv + 3 FC.
  • Slides ki line "VGG used 19 hidden layers and 144 million parameters" VGG-19 ki baat hai; VGG-16 = 138M.

Dimaag me aise baitha lo

"Teen-teen, do-do, aadha-aadha": 3×3 conv, 2×2 pool, har pool pe size aadha aur channels double. "2-2-3-3-3 + 3 = 16".

24.6 Inception / GoogLeNet (2014) — "kaunsa filter? sab ek saath!"

Kahani

Socho tum cricket team ke captain ho aur pitch ka mood pata nahi. Spinner daalo? Fast bowler? Medium pacer? Ek hi bowler chunna risky hai. Ek smart captain kahega: "Sabko thoda-thoda try karo, jo kaam kare uska zyada use karo."

CNN me bhi yahi dikkat hai. Har layer pe decide karna padta hai: 1×1, 3×3 ya 5×5 filter? Photo me kutta kabhi paas se (bada, poori photo me) dikhta hai, kabhi door (chhota sa kona). Chhota detail chhote filter se pakadta hai, badi shape bade filter se. Google ke Christian Szegedy aur team ne kaha: "Choose hi mat karo. Ek hi input pe 1×1, 3×3, 5×5 conv aur 3×3 max-pool sab parallel chalao, aur output ko channels ke along jod do (concatenate). Network training me khud seekh lega kaunsa raasta kitna kaam ka hai." Is block ka naam: Inception module. Is se bana network: GoogLeNet (LeNet ko salaam — capital "L"). Paper: "Going Deeper with Convolutions", Szegedy et al., 2014 (CVPR 2015). ILSVRC 2014 winner, top-5 6.67%.

Slides (Advanced CNN deck) ki line: Inception ne paradigm badla — "from simply stacking layers deeper to building wider networks that process information at multiple scales simultaneously." Naam "Inception" movie ke "we need to go deeper" meme aur "Network in Network" paper se aaya.

Step 1: Naive Inception module (seedha idea)

Input (maan lo 28×28×192) chaar branches me jaata hai, sab stride 1 + "same" padding ke saath taaki sabka H×W same rahe (warna concatenate nahi ho sakta):

  • 1×1 conv (padding 0) · 3×3 conv (padding 1) · 5×5 conv (padding 2) · 3×3 max-pool (stride 1, padding 1)
  • Fir concatenate along channels: output channels = sab branches ke channels ka jod. H×W same rehta hai.
Y = concatchannels( B1(X), B3(X), B5(X), Bpool(X) )   ⇒   Cout = C1 + C3 + C5 + Cpool
  • B = ek branch ka operation; C1, C3, C5 = un branches ke filters; Cpool = pool branch ke channels.
  • Concatenation me channels judte hain (add nahi hote). Shart: sabka H×W same ho; channels alag-alag ho sakte hain. (ResNet me ulta: shape poora same chahiye kyunki wahan addition hota hai.)

Teacher ke L12 page ka chhota example: RGB input 28×28×3; teen conv branches 4-4 filters (1×1 pad 0, 3×3 pad 1, 5×5 pad 2) aur pool branch (stride 1, pad 1) apne 3 channels rakhti hai → concat = 4 + 4 + 4 + 3 = 15 channels: output 28×28×15.

Step 2: Problem — compute ka bill phat jaata hai

Chalo numbers se samjhein (multiplications ginna)

Sawaal: Input 28×28×192. Hume 5×5 conv se 32 output channels chahiye (same padding). Kitne multiplications? Fir pehle 1×1 conv se 16 channels tak "pichkaa" (reduce) karke 5×5 lagaayein to?

  1. Ek output number banane ke liye ek 5×5×192 filter = 5·5·192 = 4,800 multiplications.
  2. Output me kitne numbers? 28·28·32 = 25,088. Isliye direct cost:
    28 · 28 · 32 · 5 · 5 · 192 = 120,422,400 ≈ 120.4 million
  3. Bottleneck raasta, step A — 1×1 conv 192 → 16: har output number = 1·1·192 multiplications:
    28 · 28 · 16 · 192 = 2,408,448 ≈ 2.4 million
  4. Step B — ab 5×5 conv sirf 16 channels pe:
    28 · 28 · 32 · 5 · 5 · 16 = 10,035,200 ≈ 10.0 million
  5. Total: 2,408,448 + 10,035,200 = 12,443,648 ≈ 12.4 million. Bachat: 120,422,400 / 12,443,648 ≈ 9.7× (lagbhag 10 guna sasta).

Jawab: direct ≈ 120.4M vs 1×1 bottleneck ke saath ≈ 12.4M multiplications. Output shape dono me same: 28×28×32.

Naive module ki doosri problem: pool branch input ke saare channels (192) wapas de deti hai. To naive module ka output = 64 + 128 + 32 + 192 = 416 channels — har module ke baad channels badhte jaayenge aur agla module aur mehnga. Hamare example ke naive 3a (1×1→64, 3×3→128, 5×5→32 seedha 192 channels pe) ki cost ≈ 303M multiplications; bottleneck wale asli 3a ki ≈ 128M.

Step 3: Hero — 1×1 convolution

Definition

1×1 convolution: kernel ka spatial size 1×1 hai, par depth = saare input channels (1×1×Cin). Har pixel position pe ye us pixel ke saare channels ka weighted sum leta hai (+ bias, fir ReLU). Matlab har pixel par ek chhota sa fully connected layer across channels — wahi weights har position pe. Isliye "Network in Network" (Lin, Chen & Yan, 2013) se idea aaya.

Chalo numbers se samjhein (teacher ke L12 page se)

Ek position pe 4 input channels ki values: 2, 0, 1, 3. Ek 1×1 filter ke weights: ½, ¼, 0, ½ (bias 0).

  1. ½·2 + ¼·0 + 0·1 + ½·3 = 1 + 0 + 0 + 1.5 = 2.5
  2. Doosra filter apne weights se doosra channel banata hai. 16 filters → 16 output channels. Same filters har position pe lagte hain.

Jawab: output = 2.5. 1×1 conv ne 4 numbers ko 1 me "mix" kar diya — padosi pixels ko nahi dekha.

  • Depth badalta hai, H×W nahi: 28×28×192 → (16 filters) → 28×28×16. Channel reduction ("bottleneck") ya expansion dono.
  • Params kam: (1·1·Cin + 1)·Cout. 192 → 16: (192 + 1)·16 = 3,088.
  • Non-linearity add karta hai: har 1×1 ke baad ReLU → network aur expressive, almost free.
  • Spatial receptive field nahi badhata (sirf ek position dekhta hai). Aur ye "depthwise" nahi hai — standard 1×1 saare channels mix karta hai.

Teacher ka L12 example (parameters ginna, 64 channels)

Input 28×28×64, chahiye 28×28×32 via 5×5.

  1. Direct: ek filter = 5·5·64 = 1,600 weights + 1 bias = 1,601; 32 filters → 1,601 × 32 = 51,232.
  2. Reduce pehle (1×1, 16 filters): (1·1·64 + 1)·16 = 1,040.
  3. Fir 5×5 on 16 channels: (5·5·16 + 1)·32 = 401·32 = 12,832.
  4. Jod: 1,040 + 12,832 = 13,872.

Jawab: 51,232 → 13,872 params (same output shape). Kyun sasta? Kyunki ab har 5×5 filter 64 ki jagah sirf 16 channels span karta hai. (L12 quiz ka jawab yahi tha.)

Worksheet ka 3×3 branch (weights only, bias nahi): direct 192 → 128 = 9 · 192 · 128 = 221,184. Pehle r = 96 tak reduce: 192·96 + 9·96·128 = 18,432 + 110,592 = 129,024 → 41.7% kam. Par dhyan: bottleneck hamesha sasta nahi! Sasta tabhi jab r(Cin + k²Cout) < k²CinCout. Yahan break-even r = 221,184 / (192 + 1,152) ≈ 164.6; agar r = 192 rakha to 258,048 weights — ulta mehnga. Aur bahut chhota r information bhi kho sakta hai (bottleneck = sankri gali).

Step 4: Asli Inception module (v1, dimension reduction ke saath)

Dhyan do: pool branch me 1×1 conv pool ke baad lagta hai ("pool projection") — taaki pool branch 192 channels wapas na de, sirf 32 de. Aur 3×3 / 5×5 ke pehle 1×1 lagta hai. Asli 3a ke params: (192+1)·64 + (192+1)·96 + (9·96+1)·128 + (192+1)·16 + (25·16+1)·32 + (192+1)·32 = 163,696 (naive module ke 387,296 ke mukable).

Output check (3b): 128 + 192 + 96 + 64 = 480 ✓. Rule: output = 1×1 + 3×3 + 5×5 + pool proj (reduce wale numbers output me nahi judte — wo andar ke hain).

  • Depth: 22 layers (sirf parameter wali layers ginein; pooling bhi ginein to 27). 9 inception modules.
  • Params: paper ke table ka jod ≈ 6.8M; paper kehta hai AlexNet se 12× kam params (≈5M). torchvision version (bina aux) = 6,624,904. Matlab VGG ke 138M ke saamne ~20× chhota, phir bhi zyada accurate! Inference budget ~1.5 billion multiply-adds.

Global Average Pooling (GAP) — bade FC head ki chhutti

GAP:   zc = 1H·W Σi,j Ac[i, j]    →   (H×W×C) se C numbers
  • Ac = channel c ka feature map; zc = us poore map ka ek average number. 0 parameters.

Chalo numbers se samjhein

  1. Teacher ke L12 page me GoogLeNet ka feature map #6 (7×7 = 49 values) ka jod 339.586 tha: z₆ = 339.586 / 49 = 6.930. Aise 1024 channels → 1024 numbers.
  2. Agar VGG ki tarah flatten + FC karte: 7·7·1024 = 50,176 inputs → 1000 classes: (50,176 + 1)·1000 = 50,177,000 params.
  3. GAP ke baad: (1,024 + 1)·1000 = 1,025,000 params. Bachat ≈ 49×.

Jawab: GAP se classifier ~50M se ~1M params pe aa gaya. Fayde: kam params, kam overfitting, aur input size thoda alag ho tab bhi chal jaata hai. (Idea: Network in Network, 2013. ResNet bhi yahi use karta hai.)

PyTorch me: nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d((1, 1)) — tum output size batate ho (1×1), kernel wo khud nikaal leta hai; input chahe 7×7 ho ya 4×4. Uske baad nn.Flatten() → (N, C). (torch.mean(x, dim=(2, 3)) bhi same kaam karta hai.)

Auxiliary classifiers — beech me "chhote teachers"

22 layers us zamane me bahut gehra tha; darr tha ki vanishing gradient (Chapter 13) se shuruaati layers tak signal nahi pahunchega. Jugaad: beech me (4a aur 4d ke output pe) do chhote classifiers lagao: 5×5 avg-pool (stride 3) → 1×1 conv 128 → FC 1024 → dropout 70% → FC 1000 softmax. Ye bhi same label predict karte hain aur unka loss 0.3 weight ke saath total loss me judta hai:

Ltotal = Lmain + 0.3 · ( Laux1 + Laux2 )
  • Aux losses beech ki layers ko seedha extra gradient dete hain (aur thoda regularization). Inference/test time pe aux classifiers hata diye jaate hain — prediction sirf main classifier se.

PyTorch: InceptionModule class

Naya API: torch.cat(tensors, dim) — list of tensors ko ek dimension ke along jodta hai; baaki saari dimensions same honi chahiye. PyTorch shape (N, C, H, W) hai, isliye channels = dim=1. (Keras me channels last hote hain, isliye notebook me Concatenate(axis=-1) tha.)

PyTorch · Inception module (v1)

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class InceptionModule(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_ch, c1, r3, c3, r5, c5, pool_proj):
        super().__init__()
        # Branch 1: sirf 1x1
        self.b1 = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv2d(in_ch, c1, kernel_size=1), nn.ReLU(inplace=True))
        # Branch 2: 1x1 reduce -> 3x3 (padding=1 taaki 28x28 bana rahe)
        self.b2 = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(in_ch, r3, kernel_size=1), nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
            nn.Conv2d(r3, c3, kernel_size=3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(inplace=True))
        # Branch 3: 1x1 reduce -> 5x5 (padding=2)
        self.b3 = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(in_ch, r5, kernel_size=1), nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
            nn.Conv2d(r5, c5, kernel_size=5, padding=2), nn.ReLU(inplace=True))
        # Branch 4: 3x3 maxpool (stride=1, padding=1) -> 1x1 projection
        self.b4 = nn.Sequential(
            nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=3, stride=1, padding=1),
            nn.Conv2d(in_ch, pool_proj, kernel_size=1), nn.ReLU(inplace=True))

    def forward(self, x):
        y1, y2, y3, y4 = self.b1(x), self.b2(x), self.b3(x), self.b4(x)   # sab ko SAME x milta hai
        return torch.cat([y1, y2, y3, y4], dim=1)   # dim=1 = channel axis (N, C, H, W)

inc3a = InceptionModule(192, 64, 96, 128, 16, 32, 32)
x = torch.randn(1, 192, 28, 28)
out = inc3a(x)
print("branch shapes:", [tuple(b(x).shape) for b in [inc3a.b1, inc3a.b2, inc3a.b3, inc3a.b4]])
print("module output:", tuple(out.shape))
print("params:", sum(p.numel() for p in inc3a.parameters()))

Output

branch shapes: [(1, 64, 28, 28), (1, 128, 28, 28), (1, 32, 28, 28), (1, 32, 28, 28)]
module output: (1, 256, 28, 28)
params: 163696

torchvision: models.googlenet(weights=None, aux_logits=True). Train mode me ye ek GoogLeNetOutputs deta hai jisme .logits, .aux_logits1, .aux_logits2 hote hain; eval mode me sirf logits tensor. Loss aise:

PyTorch · GoogLeNet training loss with auxiliary heads

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torchvision import models

g = models.googlenet(weights=None, aux_logits=True, init_weights=True)
g.train()
out = g(torch.randn(2, 3, 224, 224))           # train mode: 3 outputs
labels = torch.tensor([3, 7])
ce = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
loss = ce(out.logits, labels) + 0.3 * (ce(out.aux_logits1, labels) + ce(out.aux_logits2, labels))
print(type(out).__name__, out.logits.shape, out.aux_logits1.shape, out.aux_logits2.shape)
g.eval()
print(type(g(torch.randn(1, 3, 224, 224))).__name__)   # eval: sirf main logits

Output

GoogLeNetOutputs torch.Size([2, 1000]) torch.Size([2, 1000]) torch.Size([2, 1000])
Tensor

Inception ke baad ke versions (v2, v3, v4)

  • BN-Inception / "Inception v2" (Ioffe & Szegedy, 2015): isi paper ne Batch Normalization introduce kiya (Chapter 20); 5×5 ko do 3×3 se badla.
  • Inception v2/v3 (Szegedy et al., 2015, "Rethinking the Inception Architecture"): factorization — (a) 5×5 → do 3×3: 18 vs 25 → 28% sasta, same receptive field (VGG wala idea); (b) asymmetric: n×n → 1×n phir n×1 (3×3 → 1×3 + 3×1: 6 vs 9 → 33% sasta; 7×7 → 1×7 + 7×1). Saath me BN, label smoothing, RMSProp, 299×299 input, efficient grid-size reduction.
  • Inception v4 / Inception-ResNet (2016): inception modules + residual connections (Chapter 25 ka idea) → aur tez training. Xception (2017, "extreme inception"): depthwise separable convs (agla section).

Inception ki kamzoriyan (Advanced CNN deck)

  • Complex design: har module me bahut saare hand-picked numbers (64, 96, 128, 16, 32 ...). VGG/ResNet jaisa simple rule nahi.
  • Latency: params kam, par branching paths ka overhead → high FPS (real-time) mushkil.
  • Detection ke liye nahi bana: classification ke liye masterpiece, par "object kahan hai" ke liye sliding-window detectors hazaaron regions check karte the (computational waste) aur chhote patches dekhne se "big picture" context kho jaata tha. Isi wajah se R-CNN → Fast/Faster R-CNN (region proposals, RoI pooling, RPN) aur YOLO aaye.

Exam Radar

  • GoogLeNet = Inception v1, Szegedy et al. (Google), 2014, ILSVRC 2014 winner, 6.67% top-5.
  • Module: 1×1, 3×3, 5×5 conv + 3×3 max-pool parallel, outputs concatenated along channels (dim=1 in PyTorch). H×W same (stride 1 + same padding).
  • 1×1 conv: channel reduction (bottleneck), cross-channel mixing, extra ReLU non-linearity, spatial size same. From "Network in Network".
  • Cost example: 28×28×192 → 5×5×32: ≈120.4M mults direct vs ≈12.4M with 1×1 to 16 (≈10× less).
  • 3a: 64 + 128 + 32 + 32 = 256 channels. 22 layers deep, 9 inception modules, ~5–7M params (12× fewer than AlexNet), GAP instead of big FC, dropout 40%.
  • 2 auxiliary classifiers (after 4a, 4d), loss weight 0.3, purpose: fight vanishing gradients + regularize; removed at inference.
  • "VGG = deeper, Inception = wider / multi-scale, ResNet = shortcuts."

Galti mat karna

  • Inception branches ko add nahi karte, concatenate karte hain. Add = ResNet.
  • Module ke output channels me "reduce" wale filters (96, 16) mat jodo — sirf branch ke aakhri outputs (64+128+32+32).
  • Pooling branch ka stride 1 hota hai (size same rakhne ke liye) — ye downsampling ke liye nahi hai.
  • 1×1 conv "kuch nahi karta" — galat! Wo channels mix karta hai, depth badalta hai aur ReLU ke saath non-linearity laata hai.

Dimaag me aise baitha lo

"Sabko bulao, sabki suno, sabko jodo" — 1, 3, 5, pool → concat. Aur "pehle 1×1 se patla karo, phir bada filter chalao" = bottleneck.

24.7 1×1 ka ek aur kamaal: Depthwise Separable Convolution (MobileNet idea)

Kahani

Worksheet ka kitchen example: dhaba me pehle har ingredient alag-alag taiyaar hota hai (pyaaz alag kaata, tamatar alag pees), phir aakhir me sab mila kar dish banti hai. Standard convolution ek hi step me dono kaam karta hai — padosi pixels dekhna (spatial filtering) aur channels milana (channel mixing). Depthwise separable conv ye do kaam alag karta hai, aur bahut sasta pad jaata hai.

  • Depthwise conv: har input channel pe uska apna ek k×k filter (channels mix nahi hote). M channels in → M channels out.
  • Pointwise conv: phir ek 1×1 conv jo M channels ko mila kar N output channels banata hai.
Pstandard = k²MN   |   Pseparable = k²M + MN   |   PseparablePstandard = 1N + 1k²
  • M = input channels, N = output channels, k = kernel size; sirf weights (bias/BN chhod ke). MACs (multiply-accumulates) chahiye to dono ko output grid H′·W′ se multiply karo.

Chalo numbers se samjhein (worksheet ke numbers)

  1. k = 3, M = 32, N = 64. Standard: 9 · 32 · 64 = 18,432.
  2. Depthwise: 9 · 32 = 288; pointwise: 32 · 64 = 2,048; total 2,336.
  3. Ratio: 2,336 / 18,432 = 0.1267 = 1/64 + 1/9 → ~7.89× kam. 28×28 output pe MACs: 14,450,688 vs 1,831,424.
  4. Worksheet ka "check yourself": 3×3, 64 → 128: 9·64·128 = 73,728 vs 9·64 + 64·128 = 576 + 8,192 = 8,768 → ~8.41× kam.

Jawab: depthwise separable ≈ 8–9× sasta (3×3 kernels ke liye ratio ≈ 1/9 jab N bada ho). Trade-off: har filter "D[u,v,m]·P[m,n]" jaisa factorized form hi ban sakta hai — expressivity kam; accuracy aur device pe asli speed measure karni padti hai.

Worksheet ka chhota numeric: do 3×3 channels A = [1..9] aur B = [9..1], har channel pe 2×2 all-ones depthwise filter (stride 1, valid) → A′ top-left = 1+2+4+5 = 12, B′ top-left = 9+8+6+5 = 28; pointwise weights [1, −1] → 1·12 + (−1)·28 = −16. Channels pehli baar pointwise step me mile.

PyTorch me depthwise = nn.Conv2d(M, M, k, groups=M). groups argument channels ko groups me baant deta hai; groups=M → har channel akela (AlexNet ka 2-GPU split = groups=2 tha).

PyTorch · standard vs depthwise separable

import torch.nn as nn
standard = nn.Conv2d(32, 64, kernel_size=3, padding=1, bias=False)
depthwise = nn.Conv2d(32, 32, kernel_size=3, padding=1, groups=32, bias=False)  # har channel ka apna 3x3
pointwise = nn.Conv2d(32, 64, kernel_size=1, bias=False)                        # 1x1: channels mix
count = lambda m: sum(p.numel() for p in m.parameters())
print("standard :", count(standard))
print("depthwise:", count(depthwise), "| pointwise:", count(pointwise),
      "| total:", count(depthwise) + count(pointwise))
print("ratio    :", round((count(depthwise) + count(pointwise)) / count(standard), 4))

Output

standard : 18432
depthwise: 288 | pointwise: 2048 | total: 2336
ratio    : 0.1267

Exam Radar

  • Depthwise separable = depthwise (k²M) + pointwise 1×1 (MN); ratio = 1/N + 1/k². MobileNet (Howard et al., 2017) ne popular kiya; Xception bhi isi pe.
  • Channels pointwise step me mix hote hain, depthwise me nahi. Depthwise separable ≠ spatially separable (3×1 + 1×3).
